    Solutions library

    131 ways to protect people
    from heat, and what each needs.

    Passive cooling, active cooling, and the plans, rules and money that make protection last, gathered from around the world with a focus on South and Southeast Asia. Each one says how it works, whether it suits dry or humid heat, what it has done, what it costs, who acts and what could stop it.

    How to read this. It is a rapid evidence map, not a ranking. The label on each solution is the strongest kind of evidence we found for it, not a score. A label describes the evidence, not how good the solution is. Most solutions have not been independently evaluated for health or income effects; each one says what is known, what is inferred and what is uncertain.

    131 solutions

    Passive cooling 52

    Ways to keep heat out or let it escape with little or no energy: roofs, shade, walls, air flow, trees, water and design.

    Solar-reflective roof coatingsPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyReflect more incoming sunlight, reducing absorbed solar heat and heat conducted through the roof.

    How it works

    Reflect more incoming sunlight, reducing absorbed solar heat and heat conducted through the roof. High thermal emittance can also help reject absorbed heat.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates: solar rejection does not require dry air; humidity, soiling and roof construction still affect delivered benefit.

    What it has done

    • measured About 1°C lower mean indoor air temperature for painted tin versus unpainted tin. Ahmedabad, India, 4–10 October 2017; publication 2020. 16 households overall: one painted-roof intervention compared with three controls on its comparison day; seven daytime hours. Limits: Non-randomised houses; repeated sensor readings are not independent households; no health endpoint. Ahmedabad informal-settlement roof study, Vellingiri et al. (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Compatible, sound roof; correct preparation and application; maintenance and access.

    What could stop it

    Fragile sheets, leaks, insecure tenure and product quality need checking. Existing asbestos cannot safely be disturbed by untrained workers.

    Rough cost

    • Upfront: 20–40 INR per ft² (about US$0.284–0.568, per ft²). Indicative material range from manufacturer interactions, not installed household quote

    Prices from 2019. 2019 indicative Indian market information, published May 2020; labour/tax/preparation not separately specified. Running/upkeep prices not disclosed. NRDC/ASCI/IIIT-H cool-roof FAQ (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Upkeep

    Agree who checks condition, cleans safely and renews the coating; actual interval is product- and exposure-dependent.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public-facility budget; grants/subsidies where occupants cannot afford capital or are tenants. These are funding options, not verified commitments.

    Fairness and risks

    Screen who can access the roof and who bears work-at-height risk. Include tenants and women doing home-based work; avoid treating coating as proof a home is safe.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Ahmedabad, India, October 2017; published 2020. Painted tin roof compared with control roofs. One coated-roof household in 16-house study Ahmedabad informal-settlement roof study, Vellingiri et al. (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Kerail/Karail, Dhaka, Bangladesh, 2021 account; programme selected in 2019. Reflective-paint deployment described by implementation partners. 105 buildings and two garment factories selected; completed extent not separately established SEforALL programme account: Bangladesh and Indonesia (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study Small Ahmedabad comparison recorded indoor air temperature; does not establish population-wide effects. Ahmedabad informal-settlement roof study, Vellingiri et al. (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Bangladesh programme deployed reflective paint on selected buildings; results were supplied by programme partners. SEforALL programme account: Bangladesh and Indonesia (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check roof assembly, occupation schedule, sun exposure, humidity, night temperatures, local material standards and tenure. Field thermal benefits do not establish medical benefit or eliminate need for other protection.

    Other sources

    • NRDC/ASCI/IIIT-H cool-roof FAQ (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Reflective coatings have measured thermal evidence in India and reported deployment in humid Bangladesh.

    Inferred: Taxonomy links and proposed responsibilities identify plausible pathways; they are not measured cycle-breaking impacts.

    Uncertain: Installed lifecycle costs, long-term performance, health and income effects, and locally equitable access require verification.

    On the map, it can help break: The global cooling loop · The cooling trap · The energy-poverty trap · The sleepless-nights loop

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities · Markets and neighbourhoods · Before summer: for municipalities

    Reflective single-ply roof membranesPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyA light, solar-reflective sheet forms the exposed roof surface and reduces solar absorption; seams and attachment provide the waterproofing system.

    How it works

    A light, solar-reflective sheet forms the exposed roof surface and reduces solar absorption; seams and attachment provide the waterproofing system.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates in principle; aged reflectance, waterproofing and moisture design matter. Cold-climate energy findings cannot be copied to tropical housing.

    What it has done

    • reported Programme reported average indoor air temperature 2°C lower in membrane-roof homes than similar untreated homes. Hyderabad, India, May 2017 pilot; July 2019 account. 25 roofs in pilot; sensor sample count not stated. Limits: Implementation factsheet; no independent evaluation or sensor protocol available here. NRDC: Keeping It Cool, July 2019 programme factsheet (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Compatible roof substrate, skilled seam/attachment design, drainage and reliable material specification.

    What could stop it

    Upfront procurement, repairs, wind uplift, roof access and installer capacity require checking.

    Rough cost

    • Upfront: 20–55 INR per ft² (about US$0.284–0.781, per ft²). Indicative material range, not installed quote

    Prices from 2019. Indian manufacturer-market range collected 2019 and published 2020. No universal payback inferred. NRDC/ASCI/IIIT-H cool-roof FAQ (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Upkeep

    Roof owner/contractor checks seams, drainage, punctures and surface condition; repairability evidence is product-specific.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public-facility budget; grants/subsidies where occupants cannot afford capital or are tenants. These are funding options, not verified commitments.

    Fairness and risks

    Screen affordability, landlord consent, wind/fire compliance and plastic waste. No water-based cooling or operational refrigerant is inherent to the membrane.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Hyderabad, India, May 2017; account July 2019. HDPE membrane cool-roof pilot in a low-income neighbourhood. 25 city roofs NRDC: Keeping It Cool, July 2019 programme factsheet (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study United States, multiple sites, 2020 publication; installations principally 2005–2006. Existing membrane roofs sampled for durability and repair welding; individual sites not resolved in accessible text. 20 roofs, one manufacturer Keegan, Taylor and Kirby, field-aged TPO roofs (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Reported, not evaluated Hyderabad pilot installed HDPE cool-roof membrane supplied through CSR. NRDC: Keeping It Cool, July 2019 programme factsheet (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Industry-associated field study inspected aged membranes from twenty US roofs; durability, not cooling-health effectiveness, was assessed. Keegan, Taylor and Kirby, field-aged TPO roofs (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check roof assembly, occupation schedule, sun exposure, humidity, night temperatures, local material standards and tenure. Field thermal benefits do not establish medical benefit or eliminate need for other protection.

    Other sources

    • NRDC/ASCI/IIIT-H cool-roof FAQ (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Physical mechanism and installed membrane studies verified.

    Inferred: Taxonomy links and proposed responsibilities identify plausible pathways; they are not measured cycle-breaking impacts.

    Uncertain: Installed lifecycle costs, long-term performance, health and income effects, and locally equitable access require verification.

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities · Markets and neighbourhoods · Before summer: for municipalities

    Bulk roof insulation, including beneath metal sheetsPassive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataLow-conductivity material slows conductive heat flow through the roof.

    How it works

    Low-conductivity material slows conductive heat flow through the roof. It is different from a thin radiant foil and does not remove internal heat.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates with an assembly designed for local moisture and ventilation; humid climates require particular condensation control.

    What it has done

    • measured Experimental bamboo-layer slab configuration reported 53% reduction in peak heat gain at the selected insulation thickness. University of Moratuwa, Sri Lanka, First week September 2018; published 2019. Small physical roof-slab models; one experimental site. Limits: Material/assembly-specific peak heat gain; not indoor air or health outcome. Chandra et al., roof insulation experiment, Sri Lanka (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Continuous insulation, suitable material, structural/fire/electrical checks and a way to remove accumulated internal heat.

    What could stop it

    Compressed or wet insulation, thermal bridges, poorly detailed vapour layers, roof leaks and affordability.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price or cost saving inferred.

    Upkeep

    Building owner maintains weatherproofing and has wet/damaged sections checked; material-specific replacement intervals would be worth establishing.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public-facility budget; grants/subsidies where occupants cannot afford capital or are tenants. These are funding options, not verified commitments.

    Fairness and risks

    Screen foam blowing-agent/emissions information, fire behaviour, installation exposure, waste and moisture. Check affordability and permission rather than assuming tenants can modify a roof.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Moratuwa, Sri Lanka, 2018 trial; published 2019. Experimental low-conductivity roof layer. Small roof-slab physical models Chandra et al., roof insulation experiment, Sri Lanka (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test Small physical roof models tested a bamboo insulation layer beneath/within a slab assembly. Chandra et al., roof insulation experiment, Sri Lanka (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Government guidance distinguishes bulk and reflective insulation and warns about moisture, electrical and material issues. Australian Government YourHome: insulation (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check roof assembly, occupation schedule, sun exposure, humidity, night temperatures, local material standards and tenure. Field thermal benefits do not establish medical benefit or eliminate need for other protection.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Insulation physics is established; a tropical roof-slab experiment is verified.

    Inferred: Taxonomy links and proposed responsibilities identify plausible pathways; they are not measured cycle-breaking impacts.

    Uncertain: Installed lifecycle costs, long-term performance, health and income effects, and locally equitable access require verification.

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities · Markets and neighbourhoods · Before summer: for municipalities

    Secondary or false ceiling with an air gapPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyA secondary ceiling separates occupants from the hot roof and creates an intervening air layer.

    How it works

    A secondary ceiling separates occupants from the hot roof and creates an intervening air layer. The material and air-gap arrangement determine conductive and radiant heat transfer.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates, provided moisture, ceiling height and ventilation are considered; does not dehumidify hot-humid air.

    What it has done

    • measured Intervention and asbestos-control means differ by 2.38°C (researcher subtraction); authors described the difference approximately as 2.5°C. Ahmedabad, India, October 2017; publication 2020. One intervention and three controls; 16 homes overall. Limits: Non-randomised cross-house comparison. Derived subtraction of reported means, not a paired estimate; no health endpoint. Ahmedabad informal-settlement roof study, Vellingiri et al. (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • modelled A clinic model with a 0.20 m passive ceiling gap predicted 2.54°C lower mean room temperature versus no false ceiling. Bangladesh clinic archetype, 2026 publication. One numerical single-storey clinic archetype. Limits: Modelled, not installed outcome; active ventilation/PV results excluded. Muna et al., Bangladesh clinic false-ceiling modelling (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Safe ceiling support, sufficient room height and a roof/ceiling detail that does not create condensation or restrict necessary ventilation.

    What could stop it

    Combustible exposed foam, low room height, leaks, maintenance access and unsafe wiring require review.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price or cost saving inferred.

    Upkeep

    Owner or public-facility manager checks suspension, dampness, pests and wiring; establish local inspection schedule.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public-facility budget; grants/subsidies where occupants cannot afford capital or are tenants. These are funding options, not verified commitments.

    Fairness and risks

    Screen fire safety and avoid presenting exposed Thermocol as a universal DIY recommendation. Consider renters, home-based workers and accessibility during installation.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Ahmedabad, India, 2017; published 2020. Secondary Thermocol ceiling was installed and monitored. One household intervention Ahmedabad informal-settlement roof study, Vellingiri et al. (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study Ahmedabad household temperature comparison included a Thermocol false ceiling. Ahmedabad informal-settlement roof study, Vellingiri et al. (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Published numerical analysis simulated passive ceiling-gap cases; evidence label measured describes an analysis, while effect basis is modelled. Muna et al., Bangladesh clinic false-ceiling modelling (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check roof assembly, occupation schedule, sun exposure, humidity, night temperatures, local material standards and tenure. Field thermal benefits do not establish medical benefit or eliminate need for other protection.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: One small installed household comparison and a separate numerical clinic analysis are verified.

    Inferred: Taxonomy links and proposed responsibilities identify plausible pathways; they are not measured cycle-breaking impacts.

    Uncertain: Installed lifecycle costs, long-term performance, health and income effects, and locally equitable access require verification.

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities · Markets and neighbourhoods · Before summer: for municipalities

    Low-emissivity radiant barrier beneath roof or ceilingPassive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataA low-emissivity facing reduces radiant heat exchange across an adjacent air space.

    How it works

    A low-emissivity facing reduces radiant heat exchange across an adjacent air space. It is not equivalent to bulk insulation when pressed between materials.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates; incoming roof radiation occurs in dry and humid heat. Air gap, dust and moisture details govern performance.

    What it has done

    • reported The project reported monitoring and barrier installation but did not disclose a numeric thermal-effect estimate on the reviewed page. Jaipur, India, February 2024–January 2025; account November 2025. Three monitored buildings; barrier/coating mock-up in one. Limits: Project communications; manuscript then in preparation. Mittal Institute/MNIT Jaipur radiant-barrier project account (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Specified reflective surface and air space, correct orientation/detailing, safe separation from electrical equipment.

    What could stop it

    Foil in contact with live wiring, dust, condensation, fire performance and loss of required air space.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price or cost saving inferred.

    Upkeep

    Owner/installer preserves the air gap and checks damage, dust and moisture when safely accessible; no universal renewal cycle verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public-facility budget; grants/subsidies where occupants cannot afford capital or are tenants. These are funding options, not verified commitments.

    Fairness and risks

    Conductive foil is an electrical hazard if badly installed. Screen access and retrofit affordability; this is not a safe-working-temperature guarantee.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Jaipur, India, 2024–2025. MNIT/Harvard-associated project tested radiant barriers; numeric results unavailable in reviewed account. One installed mock-up within three monitored buildings Mittal Institute/MNIT Jaipur radiant-barrier project account (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test Jaipur project installed lightweight ceiling-hung radiant barriers and a cool-roof coating in one test building. Mittal Institute/MNIT Jaipur radiant-barrier project account (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Government guidance describes reflective-airspace mechanism and electrical/condensation precautions. Australian Government YourHome: insulation (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check roof assembly, occupation schedule, sun exposure, humidity, night temperatures, local material standards and tenure. Field thermal benefits do not establish medical benefit or eliminate need for other protection.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Installed Jaipur mock-up and established radiant-airspace mechanism verified.

    Inferred: Taxonomy links and proposed responsibilities identify plausible pathways; they are not measured cycle-breaking impacts.

    Uncertain: Installed lifecycle costs, long-term performance, health and income effects, and locally equitable access require verification.

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities · Markets and neighbourhoods · Before summer: for municipalities

    Ventilated double-skin roofPassive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataAn outer roof intercepts sunlight while an open cavity allows wind/buoyancy to remove some heat before it reaches the inner roof.

    How it works

    An outer roof intercepts sunlight while an open cavity allows wind/buoyancy to remove some heat before it reaches the inner roof. This entry includes attic/roof-space ventilation rather than counting it again.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates if openings admit airflow without rain; cavity ventilation does not itself remove indoor humidity.

    What it has done

    • measured Ventilated small-scale model reported indoor air temperature 4.8°C below its control in the clearly stated main comparison. Parit Raja, Batu Pahat, Johor, Malaysia, Published January 2024; measurement calendar dates not reported in abstract. Small-scale model configurations at UTHM; at least three measurement days stated. Limits: Abstract also presents differing summaries; full PDF was not accessible; avoid transferring magnitude to full-scale homes. Lawin and Zakaria, small-scale roof field study (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Continuous inlet/outlet path, suitable roof pitch and wind/rain/structural design; keep occupant ventilation separate from cavity flow.

    What could stop it

    Blocked cavity, rain penetration, uplift, fire spread paths, extra load and unaffordable roof replacement.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price or cost saving inferred.

    Upkeep

    Owner/roofer maintains inlet/outlet clearance, screens, fixings and rain details; inspect after damage and according to local guidance.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public-facility budget; grants/subsidies where occupants cannot afford capital or are tenants. These are funding options, not verified commitments.

    Fairness and risks

    Check cyclone exposure, pests, birds, fire breaks and access. Do not transfer model-cell temperature changes to occupied housing.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Parit Raja, Johor, Malaysia, 2024 publication. Ventilated double-roof configuration tested against control. Small-scale university field models Lawin and Zakaria, small-scale roof field study (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test UTHM small-scale roof models compared ventilated, reflective and insulation cases. Lawin and Zakaria, small-scale roof field study (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Government passive-cooling guidance explains ventilation of roof buffer spaces. Australian Government YourHome: passive cooling (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check roof assembly, occupation schedule, sun exposure, humidity, night temperatures, local material standards and tenure. Field thermal benefits do not establish medical benefit or eliminate need for other protection.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Small prototype test and mechanism verified.

    Inferred: Taxonomy links and proposed responsibilities identify plausible pathways; they are not measured cycle-breaking impacts.

    Uncertain: Installed lifecycle costs, long-term performance, health and income effects, and locally equitable access require verification.

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities · Markets and neighbourhoods · Before summer: for municipalities

    Independent over-roof shade, including ventilated PV shadePassive coolingDry and humid heatSimulation or testAn elevated canopy intercepts solar radiation before it reaches the original roof.

    How it works

    An elevated canopy intercepts solar radiation before it reaches the original roof. A ventilated gap helps avoid trapping heated air; PV electricity production is separate from this passive shading function.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates in principle; geometry, clear airflow and weather resistance govern transfer.

    What it has done

    • measured The roof surface beneath an experimental solar panel was cooler than the exposed grey reference during midday on most days; no numeric underlying-roof difference extracted. Shenzhen, China, December 2017–July 2018; published 2020. One rooftop experiment; one panel and comparison surfaces. Limits: Panel surface itself warmed at midday. Does not demonstrate lower neighbourhood air temperature or health benefit. Chen et al., four roof surfaces, Shenzhen (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Engineered attachment, spacing and roof access; for PV, include electrical safety and distinguish electricity benefit from passive cooling.

    What could stop it

    Wind uplift, extra load, conflicts with roof uses, tenure, fire access and heat trapped under a poorly ventilated cover.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price or cost saving inferred.

    Upkeep

    Roof owner/canopy operator maintains fixings, clearances, drainage and safe access. PV system maintenance is additional.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public-facility budget; grants/subsidies where occupants cannot afford capital or are tenants. These are funding options, not verified commitments.

    Fairness and risks

    Ask who owns roof space and who receives electricity/thermal benefits. Consider maintenance access, waste and possible hot upper surfaces; no zero-impact claim.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Shenzhen, China, 2017–2018 campaign; publication 2020. Panel shading provides an example of independent over-roof shading. One research-rooftop panel experiment Chen et al., four roof surfaces, Shenzhen (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test Research rooftop measured both panel and underlying-surface temperature; shading cooled the underlying surface. Chen et al., four roof surfaces, Shenzhen (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check roof assembly, occupation schedule, sun exposure, humidity, night temperatures, local material standards and tenure. Field thermal benefits do not establish medical benefit or eliminate need for other protection.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Underlying-roof shading effect measured in one experiment.

    Inferred: Taxonomy links and proposed responsibilities identify plausible pathways; they are not measured cycle-breaking impacts.

    Uncertain: Installed lifecycle costs, long-term performance, health and income effects, and locally equitable access require verification.

    On the map, it can help break: The displacement loop

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities · Markets and neighbourhoods · Before summer: for municipalities

    Vegetated or green roofPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyPlants shade the roof, while growing substrate changes heat flow and evapotranspiration uses available water.

    How it works

    Plants shade the roof, while growing substrate changes heat flow and evapotranspiration uses available water. Irrigation and drainage can add resource and operational requirements.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both only conditionally: dry settings need an explicit water budget; humid settings still experience dry spells and reduced evapotranspiration potential.

    What it has done

    • measured Advanced ventilated grass-tray roof had mean rooftop surface temperature 3.00°C below bare roof over the monitored daytime period. Bangkok, Thailand, 2026 publication; field calendar date not disclosed. Three 1.215 m³ test chambers, ten daytime hours. Limits: Combined vegetation and ventilation; tiny chambers, not occupied buildings; daily watering. Ventilated grass-tray test, Bangkok (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • measured Grass surface averaged only 0.43°C cooler than grey reference across the study period, with performance constrained by soil moisture. Shenzhen, China, December 2017–July 2018; published 2020. Four surfaces at one research-building rooftop. Limits: Surface metric; does not measure indoor air or health. Chen et al., four roof surfaces, Shenzhen (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Structural capacity, waterproofing, drainage, suitable plants, reliable care and a water source compatible with local scarcity.

    What could stop it

    Water shortage, saturated roof load, leaks, dying plants, maintenance cost and insecure tenure.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price or cost saving inferred.

    Upkeep

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Screen water competition, roof access, mosquito/pest management, safe drainage and who benefits. Roof greening does not justify tenant displacement or rent increases.

    A reflective tile/mosaic finish reduces solar absorption at the roof surface. It is a durable surface assembly rather than a liquid coating or a single-ply membrane.

    Solar-control low-e glazing and secondary-glazing retrofitsPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyGlazing selection changes solar transmission and long-wave heat exchange; a secondary pane adds a thermal barrier.

    How it works

    Glazing selection changes solar transmission and long-wave heat exchange; a secondary pane adds a thermal barrier. Low emissivity alone is not proof of low solar gain.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both, with specification: select solar heat-gain coefficient and daylight together; added insulation does not replace ventilation or control indoor heat sources.

    What it has done

    • modelled Best reported scenario produced 5.9% modelled annual HVAC energy savings. Singapore, 2020. One testbed office room plus simulated glazing/orientation scenarios. Limits: Best-case simulation with 8% window-to-envelope ratio; field tests measured optical/heat-flux changes, not this annual saving. Somasundaram et al., tropical low-e secondary-glazing test and model (article mirror) (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Design is checked against sun exposure, construction and use; safe installation and continuing access are agreed.

    What could stop it

    Screen permissions, insecure tenure, landlord–tenant incentives, unsafe access and installation quality.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no global price inferred.

    Upkeep

    No transferable service life or maintenance interval verified. Proposed responsible party: owner or agreed maintenance provider; inspect fixings, surfaces and operability according to product/site requirements.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed options: property owner, public housing/education budget, employer or grant support; no financing commitment implied. Tenants cannot safely be assumed to finance capital improvements.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess affordability, tenant rights, gendered use of rooms and controls, disability access, privacy, fire escape and safe installation. No refrigerant is needed for the passive component; embodied impacts and disposal still require assessment.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Singapore, 2020 publication. Hard-coat low-e secondary panes installed and monitored. One office testbed with three facade orientations Somasundaram et al., tropical low-e secondary-glazing test and model (article mirror) (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test Field testbed studied sequential retrofit configurations; simulations estimated annual savings. Somasundaram et al., tropical low-e secondary-glazing test and model (article mirror) (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Indian residential envelope guidance treats glazing, shading and opening dimensions together. BEE: Eco-Niwas Samhita building-envelope guidance (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer the mechanism, not the reported effect size: check orientation, glazing/roof balance, ventilation, climate, occupancy and maintenance capacity.

    Window area and orientation change solar exposure, while openable area affects ventilation potential. Design would ideally balance solar exclusion with useful light and air.

    Dry and humid heat. Both: use local sun path and ventilation needs; reducing glazing indiscriminately may worsen daylight and airflow, especially in humid crowded rooms.

    Design is checked against sun exposure, construction and use; safe installation and continuing access are agreed.

    What could stop it

    Climbing-plant green facades and trellisesPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyFoliage shades the facade; evapotranspiration and the air layer alter heat and moisture exchange.

    How it works

    Foliage shades the facade; evapotranspiration and the air layer alter heat and moisture exchange. Cooler leaves or wall surfaces do not guarantee cooler occupied air.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both conditionally: shading transfers across climates; dry climates require a sustainable water source, while humid climates require checking added humidity and airflow.

    What it has done

    • measured Climbing facade room was around 1 °C cooler; cooling-energy savings reached up to 35%. Hanoi, Vietnam, July–August 2018; published 2019. Two similar rooms in one tube house; Bougainvillea on one facade. Limits: Small non-randomised room comparison; no universal effect or causal health estimate. Nguyen et al., green facade on Hanoi tube house (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • measured Green-screen cavities were up to 8 °C cooler during sunlit periods, with higher humidity. Santiago, Chile, Summer measurements; published 2020. Four buildings, orientations and plant conditions. Limits: Cavity air, not occupied-room or street-air temperature; study found reversal later in day/night. Vasquez et al.: four Santiago green screen facades (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Design is checked against sun exposure, construction and use; safe installation and continuing access are agreed.

    What could stop it

    Screen permissions, insecure tenure, landlord–tenant incentives, unsafe access and installation quality.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no global price inferred.

    Upkeep

    Agree who irrigates, prunes, replaces failed plants, checks trellis anchorage and maintains access. No universal frequency or plant lifespan verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed options: property owner, public housing/education budget, employer or grant support; no financing commitment implied. Tenants cannot safely be assumed to finance capital improvements.

    Fairness and risks

    Check water demand, drought mortality, wet-wall detailing, species suitability, pests, safe pruning and public/tenant access. Ask whether improvements could increase rents or displace users; displacement was not measured in the cited facade studies.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Hanoi, Vietnam, 2018. Climbing Bougainvillea facade monitored. One tube house; two rooms Nguyen et al., green facade on Hanoi tube house (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Santiago, Chile, 2020 publication. Green screens observed across orientations and maturity levels. Four buildings Vasquez et al.: four Santiago green screen facades (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study Occupied-building paired-room measurements. Nguyen et al., green facade on Hanoi tube house (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Four-building cavity observations. Vasquez et al.: four Santiago green screen facades (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Scale models showed that lower temperature can coincide with higher humidity and poorer effective-temperature comfort. Widiastuti et al., green-facade scale-model measurements (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer the mechanism, not the reported effect size: check orientation, glazing/roof balance, ventilation, climate, occupancy and maintenance capacity.

    Other sources

    • Hecht et al.: existing Singapore vertical greenery field research (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Cross ventilation through connected openingsPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyWind pressure differences move air between openings on different sides; when incoming air is favourable it removes indoor heat and provides air movement.

    How it works

    Wind pressure differences move air between openings on different sides; when incoming air is favourable it removes indoor heat and provides air movement. It does not refrigerate incoming air.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both, conditionally: requires favourable outdoor air and a useful breeze. In hot-humid settings movement can support comfort but does not remove moisture; exclude unfavourable hot or polluted air.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Guidance and built examples support the ventilation mechanism; no isolated cross-ventilation effect with complete baseline metadata was verified. A combined Malaysian retrofit study cannot attribute its package result to ventilation alone. Not site-specific, Checked 2026-10-27. Not applicable. Limits: Jodhpur modelling addressed natural ventilation generally, not an attributable cross-ventilation treatment. Its percentage has been withheld. Australian Government Your Home: Ventilation and airtightness (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    An unobstructed airflow path, operable openings and suitable external conditions are available.

    What could stop it

    Deep plans, blocked openings, insecure windows, insect screens with excessive flow resistance, smoke, dust, rain and hot external air require local assessment.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed for the isolated measure in reviewed sources. Whole-building capital costs are not an intervention price; no USD estimate or exchange rate inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed maintenance arrangement: owner/facility manager and users keep air paths and operable elements functional; inspect after damage or blockage. Service life and routine frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public facility budget, with grant support where needed for low-income users. No financing commitment verified.

    Fairness and risks

    Check privacy, security and accessible controls; opening a door would ideally not be a condition of protection for women or vulnerable residents. No direct water or refrigerant requirement for manual openings; later fan assistance uses electricity. Displacement and rent effects were not evaluated.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Cairns, Queensland, Australia, Construction date not reported. Openings on multiple sides and a breezeway form part of a multi-measure tropical design; isolated cooling contribution not evaluated. One house Your Home: Cairns Queensland built-house case (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Malaysia; precise town not stated in institutional abstract, September–December 2018 measurements; 2020 publication. Full-day free-running ventilation was used alongside roof shade and ceiling insulation. Benefits cannot be attributed to ventilation alone. One corner terrace house Tuck et al.: Affordable retrofitting of Malaysian terrace house, Tokyo City University (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Official guidance or data Official guidance distinguishes intentional ventilation from uncontrolled leakage. Australian Government Your Home: Ventilation and airtightness (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study A Malaysian house experiment used ventilation within a combined retrofit package. Tuck et al.: Affordable retrofitting of Malaysian terrace house, Tokyo City University (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study The Jodhpur shelter analysis examined natural ventilation generally. It is retained as adjacent modelling context, not an attributable cross-ventilation effect; no percentage transferred. Wu et al.: Indoor thermal resilience of passive/low-power cooling shelters, IIHS author abstract (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer the airflow principle, not an Australian building budget or a Malaysian package effect. Test local wind, urban shielding, outdoor pollution and occupant control.

    Other sources

    • Australian Government Your Home: Passive cooling (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Stack ventilation with high and low openingsPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyA vertical temperature and density difference can make warm air exit high openings and draw replacement air through lower inlets.

    How it works

    A vertical temperature and density difference can make warm air exit high openings and draw replacement air through lower inlets. This moves air; it is not a dehumidifier.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both, conditionally: a useful buoyancy pressure difference and suitable replacement air are needed; weak temperature gradients or adverse wind can limit flow.

    What it has done

    • measured Mean measured air velocity in the air well was 0.91 m/s over the reported campaign. This is shaft velocity, not a room temperature reduction. Kuching, Malaysia, 2019 publication. One house, five measurement days. Limits: Dates within year and sensor-height aggregate not fully reported in accessed abstract; no isolated health outcome. Leng et al.: Field Investigation of Indoor Thermal Performance in Malaysia Air-Welled Terraced House (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Low inlet and high outlet are connected without excessive resistance and fire compartmentation is maintained.

    What could stop it

    Limited height, wind reversal, obstructed shafts and smoke/fire-spread requirements; roof penetrations require competent design.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed for the isolated measure in reviewed sources. Whole-building capital costs are not an intervention price; no USD estimate or exchange rate inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed maintenance arrangement: owner/facility manager and users keep air paths and operable elements functional; inspect after damage or blockage. Service life and routine frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public facility budget, with grant support where needed for low-income users. No financing commitment verified.

    Fairness and risks

    Check who can reach high controls, insect protection and privacy. A shaft reading is not an occupied-zone cooling guarantee. No deliberate water use or refrigerant, but embodied material and possible later fan use remain. Rent/displacement impacts not studied.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Kuching, Sarawak, Malaysia, 2019 publication; five-day measurement campaign. Air-well measurements examined vertical natural airflow; no controlled no-well house was reported in abstract. One single-storey terraced house Leng et al.: Field Investigation of Indoor Thermal Performance in Malaysia Air-Welled Terraced House (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Cairns, Queensland, Australia, Construction date not reported. Low louvres and high clerestory outlets are described as thermal venting within combined passive design. One house Your Home: Cairns Queensland built-house case (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study A five-day field study measured airflow and thermal variables in an existing air well. Leng et al.: Field Investigation of Indoor Thermal Performance in Malaysia Air-Welled Terraced House (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Government case describes built high/low openings. Your Home: Cairns Queensland built-house case (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Use a full airflow and fire-safety design; do not transfer a single air-well velocity to all rooms or all buildings.

    Other sources

    • Australian Government Your Home: Ventilation and airtightness (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Windcatchers / badgirs / barjeelPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyA roof-level tower captures wind pressure and directs air through a building, sometimes combining wind and buoyancy.

    How it works

    A roof-level tower captures wind pressure and directs air through a building, sometimes combining wind and buoyancy. Any water-assisted stage is an additional evaporative system, not an inherent property of the tower.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both only with climate-specific design: captured wind can improve ventilation, but a dry tower does not cool supply air below its source temperature or remove humidity.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Implementation documented, but no transferable isolated cooling magnitude verified in the reviewed sources. Not site-specific, Not reported. Not reported. Limits: No isolated health or income outcome measured. Nazir et al.: Windcatchers as a Green Ventilation Device, Hyderabad (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Tower location, height, orientation, flow path and controllable outlet suit local wind conditions.

    What could stop it

    Deterioration or disuse, neighbouring buildings blocking wind, structural permissions and roof access; restored heritage form alone does not establish current performance.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed for the isolated measure in reviewed sources. Whole-building capital costs are not an intervention price; no USD estimate or exchange rate inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed maintenance arrangement: owner/facility manager and users keep air paths and operable elements functional; inspect after damage or blockage. Service life and routine frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public facility budget, with grant support where needed for low-income users. No financing commitment verified.

    Fairness and risks

    Check dust/smoke ingress, insects, noise, accessible controls and maintenance access. Gender/privacy and landlord permission need local consultation. No direct water/refrigerant in dry operation; wet variants add water and hygiene obligations.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Hyderabad, Sindh, Pakistan, 2024 online; 2025 issue. Study compared vernacular and modern windcatchers and users’ perspectives; maintenance and fit to current needs affected acceptance. Four buildings compared Nazir et al.: Windcatchers as a Green Ventilation Device, Hyderabad (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Mortaz House, Yazd, Iran, 2020 publication; measurement dates not stated in accessed abstract. Long-term field monitoring studied inside/outside airflow relationships. No numeric cooling result extracted from the accessed abstract. One existing windcatcher Hedayat et al.: Wind flow patterns in ancient wind catchers, Mortaz house (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study Four-building comparison links modern versus deteriorated windcatcher usability to user perspectives. Nazir et al.: Windcatchers as a Green Ventilation Device, Hyderabad (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Existing Yazd windcatcher field observations establish airflow behaviour, not a transferable temperature claim. Hedayat et al.: Wind flow patterns in ancient wind catchers, Mortaz house (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Hyderabad user findings caution against transferring historical form without matching current occupancy, expectations and maintenance capacity.

    Courtyards and open air wellsPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyAn internal open space can provide shade, access to air and a route for air exchange; its geometry and openings determine whether it ventilates or instead traps heat.

    How it works

    An internal open space can provide shade, access to air and a route for air exchange; its geometry and openings determine whether it ventilates or instead traps heat.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both, with different geometry and shading needs. Humid settings need effective air exchange; dry settings can exploit shade and night heat loss. An unshaded enclosed court is not automatically cool.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Implementation documented, but no transferable isolated cooling magnitude verified in the reviewed sources. Not site-specific, Not reported. Not reported. Limits: No isolated health or income outcome measured. Leng et al.: Field Investigation of Indoor Thermal Performance in Malaysia Air-Welled Terraced House (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Shade, geometry, sky exposure, room openings and air path are designed together.

    What could stop it

    Land/space constraints, enclosure by later construction, obstructed openings, poor drainage or unshaded solar gain.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed for the isolated measure in reviewed sources. Whole-building capital costs are not an intervention price; no USD estimate or exchange rate inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed maintenance arrangement: owner/facility manager and users keep air paths and operable elements functional; inspect after damage or blockage. Service life and routine frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public facility budget, with grant support where needed for low-income users. No financing commitment verified.

    Fairness and risks

    Check step-free access, usable shared space, safety and who controls it. Vegetation or water features add maintenance/water costs and would ideally avoid displacing residents. Integrated high-cost institutional landscaping is not an affordability example.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Kuching, Sarawak, Malaysia, 2019 publication. Existing air well tested in a tropical terraced house. This is a small vertical court, not proof for all open courtyards. One house; five measurement days Leng et al.: Field Investigation of Indoor Thermal Performance in Malaysia Air-Welled Terraced House (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated SAILC, Auro University, Surat, India, 2023 project. Architect describes courtyards integrated with vegetation, water bodies and natural ventilation; no independent thermal attribution. Institutional building; 2,800 m² built-up area reported by architect Studio Naqshbandi: Sri Aurobindo Integral Life Centre, Surat (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study Small air-well field measurements show geometry-specific tropical airflow. Leng et al.: Field Investigation of Indoor Thermal Performance in Malaysia Air-Welled Terraced House (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Architect documents a built multi-measure courtyard design. Studio Naqshbandi: Sri Aurobindo Integral Life Centre, Surat (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Treat a court as a building-specific design decision, not a universal retrofit or temperature reduction. Retain flood drainage and local cultural uses.

    Earth–air tunnels / buried-air heat exchangersPassive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyIncoming air exchanges heat with cooler ground through buried ducts before entering a building.

    How it works

    Incoming air exchanges heat with cooler ground through buried ducts before entering a building. Fan-driven versions consume electricity and are conditional low-energy hybrids, not zero-energy passive systems.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Best considered where measured ground temperatures are below intake air; hot-humid feasibility is conditional on moisture, condensate drainage and ground conditions.

    What it has done

    • measured Observed inlet–outlet supply-air temperature difference could exceed 15 °C under the study conditions. Biskra University, Algeria, May–September 2013; published 2018. One PVC serpentine duct, 56 m long, internal diameter 0.110 m, buried 3 m; seasonal campaign. Limits: This is not occupied-room cooling; exact exceedance frequency, time and cooling load are not established in abstract. Earlier measurements, recent publication. Hamdi et al.: Experimental study of earth-to-air heat exchanger in arid zone (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Ground thermal properties, drainage, duct hygiene, intake quality and actual fan energy are assessed.

    What could stop it

    Excavation cost/space, groundwater, flood ingress, contaminated soil or intake air and inaccessible ducts.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed for the isolated measure in reviewed sources. Whole-building capital costs are not an intervention price; no USD estimate or exchange rate inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed maintenance arrangement: owner/facility manager and users keep air paths and operable elements functional; inspect after damage or blockage. Service life and routine frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public facility budget, with grant support where needed for low-income users. No financing commitment verified.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess mould/condensation, cleanability, flood contamination and electricity affordability. Proposed household access requires land/tenure permission. No refrigerant; dry exchange needs no evaporative water, but wet-soil hybrids may add irrigation demand.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Biskra University, Biskra, Algeria, May–September 2013 measurements; 2018 publication. Field measurements of inlet/outlet and soil temperatures; significant supply-air cooling does not establish whole-building or health benefits. One 56 m PVC buried-duct system Hamdi et al.: Experimental study of earth-to-air heat exchanger in arid zone (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study Field apparatus monitored inlet/outlet and soil temperatures; fan energy would be worth including in assessment. Hamdi et al.: Experimental study of earth-to-air heat exchanger in arid zone (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Ajmer-affiliated CFD optimisation is a modelling study, not a verified second deployment; validation used a published numerical model. Agrawal et al.: Optimization of earth air tunnel parameters, Taguchi method (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    The Biskra air-temperature difference is device inlet/outlet, not an indoor reduction. Avoid waterlogging/flood-prone sites without engineered protection; evaluate lifecycle energy, not passive branding.

    Night flushing / night-purge ventilationPassive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataWhen outdoor air is cooler than the building, opening suitable flow paths can remove stored heat at night.

    How it works

    When outdoor air is cooler than the building, opening suitable flow paths can remove stored heat at night. Fan-assisted purge is a separate powered variant; passive operation relies on wind or buoyancy.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Hot-dry most promising where nights are cooler. Hot-humid suitability would be worth checking hour by hour; warm humid nights may provide too little heat rejection and bring moisture.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Implementation documented, but no transferable isolated cooling magnitude verified in the reviewed sources. Not site-specific, Not reported. Not reported. Limits: No isolated health or income outcome measured. Australian Government Your Home: Passive cooling (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Night air offers a useful heat sink and openings can remain safely operable.

    What could stop it

    Hot nights, smoke, noise, mosquitoes, rain, burglary risk, inaccessible openings and security restrictions.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed for the isolated measure in reviewed sources. Whole-building capital costs are not an intervention price; no USD estimate or exchange rate inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed maintenance arrangement: owner/facility manager and users keep air paths and operable elements functional; inspect after damage or blockage. Service life and routine frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public facility budget, with grant support where needed for low-income users. No financing commitment verified.

    Fairness and risks

    Night opening would ideally avoid trading cooling for privacy or safety. Check people who cannot operate controls independently and whether care work increases. No deliberate water/refrigerant for manual purge; powered variants add energy and noise.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Darwin River, Northern Territory, Australia, Construction date not reported. Insect-screened windows can remain open overnight in a breezeway/low-mass tropical design; no isolated night-purge thermal effect reported. One house Your Home: Darwin River Northern Territory built-house case (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Aalborg University research context, Denmark; exact test site not established in abstract, 2021 publication. Night-ventilation heat transfer and thermal mass distribution investigated using mixing ventilation. Powered laboratory airflow is physics evidence, not a passive field deployment. Full-scale dynamic laboratory experiment Guo et al.: Experimental investigation of convective heat transfer for night ventilation (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Official guidance or data Official guidance describes removal of stored heat using cooler night air. Australian Government Your Home: Passive cooling (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Built tropical home documents overnight opening with insect screening. Your Home: Darwin River Northern Territory built-house case (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Do not use a universal diurnal threshold as a safety rule. Test local night profiles, thermal mass, weather and actual household ability to open windows.

    Shaded thermal mass with a heat-rejection strategyPassive coolingDry heatOfficial guidance or dataDense materials absorb and release heat slowly, reducing or delaying temperature swings.

    How it works

    Dense materials absorb and release heat slowly, reducing or delaying temperature swings. Stored heat is later released; adding mass without a cooler sink can prolong nighttime heat.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry heat. Hot-dry or composite climates with reliable cooler periods are the main application. In hot-humid buildings with small day-night swings, high mass is not reliably beneficial; guidance often favours low-mass construction there.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Implementation documented, but no transferable isolated cooling magnitude verified in the reviewed sources. Not site-specific, Not reported. Not reported. Limits: No isolated health or income outcome measured. Australian Government Your Home: Thermal mass (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Mass is shaded/insulated appropriately and can discharge heat to cooler air or another assessed sink.

    What could stop it

    Hot nights, solar-exposed mass, structural retrofit weight, floor-space constraints and embodied emissions.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed for the isolated measure in reviewed sources. Whole-building capital costs are not an intervention price; no USD estimate or exchange rate inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed maintenance arrangement: owner/facility manager and users keep air paths and operable elements functional; inspect after damage or blockage. Service life and routine frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: building owner or public facility budget, with grant support where needed for low-income users. No financing commitment verified.

    Fairness and risks

    Do not recommend costly heavy reconstruction as a low-cost retrofit. Check night heat burden, displacement during works, accessible space and who bears embodied-carbon/capital costs. No intrinsic refrigerant/water, but coupled systems may use both.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated White Gum Valley, Western Australia, Construction date not reported. Government case records concrete/rammed-earth mass within a combined passive/active design; no isolated mass effect. Two apartments Your Home: White Gum Valley Western Australia (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Parkside, Adelaide, South Australia, Construction date not reported. Internal rammed-earth walls and a hybrid evaporative/ventilation system use thermal storage; not a fully passive cooling package. One dwelling Your Home: Parkside South Australia (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Official guidance or data Official guidance warns that inappropriate mass can worsen comfort, particularly in humid low-range climates. Australian Government Your Home: Thermal mass (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Built apartments document material mass as part of a combined design. Your Home: White Gum Valley Western Australia (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Built house combines mass with powered evaporative cooling, not proof of a passive-only outcome. Your Home: Parkside South Australia (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer storage/discharge logic rather than Australian design costs. The Jodhpur simulation included mass but found limited additional gains from more complex packages; no isolated mass coefficient inferred.

    Other sources

    • Wu et al.: Indoor thermal resilience of passive/low-power cooling shelters, IIHS author abstract (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Raised-floor buildings and open breezewaysPassive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataElevation and a narrow/open layout can reduce wind obstruction and create routes for air to move around and through occupied areas.

    How it works

    Elevation and a narrow/open layout can reduce wind obstruction and create routes for air to move around and through occupied areas. A breezeway itself is not colder than its air source.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both conditionally, with strongest transfer from humid-tropical examples where breeze capture and avoiding trapped heat are priorities; dry hot dusty wind may be undesirable.

    What it has done

Limits: No isolated health or income outcome measured. Your Home: Cairns Queensland built-house case (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Wind exposure and internal circulation are kept clear; structure and stairs/ramps satisfy local requirements.

    What could stop it

    Dense urban plots, neighbouring buildings, cyclone/fire/structural constraints, access requirements and retrofit expense.

    Rough cost

    Fairness and risks

    Check step-free access, fall risk, disability access, safe underfloor use and rent/displacement during rebuilding. Elevation is not a flood-safe certification. No intrinsic refrigerant or water; supplementary fans/AC remain powered.

Raised floor and one-room-wide cross-shaped plan designed to capture breezes above surrounding vegetation.     Clay pot-in-pot or pot-in-dish produce coolerPassive coolingDry heatMeasured in a studyWater evaporating through a porous outer vessel removes heat; the damp sand and inner clay vessel provide a cooler, humid produce-storage microenvironment.

    How it works

    Water evaporating through a porous outer vessel removes heat; the damp sand and inner clay vessel provide a cooler, humid produce-storage microenvironment. This cools produce, not an occupied room.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry heat. Evaporation works best with a substantial wet-bulb depression; humid rainy periods reduce the available cooling.

    What it has done

    • measured During dry-season field use, cooler interiors averaged 5–7 °C below ambient; this is storage-air cooling, not human-space cooling. Mali: Bankass/Samanko programme, 2017 field phase reported in 2021. Individual devices instrumented at five-minute intervals; field device count not stated in summary. Limits: Season-specific; no household heat-health effect measured. Clay pot coolers: Mali report 2016–2021 (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Water, porous unglazed vessels, shaded ventilated siting and suitable vegetables are available.

    What could stop it

    Humid weather, insufficient water, unsuitable fired/glazed pots, breakage or unfamiliar storage routines.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal or inferred price supplied.

    Upkeep

    Users replenish water and clean/inspect vessels; replacement frequency and lifetime depend on local pottery and handling.

    Who acts

    Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Community and civil society groups, Employers and businesses. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed, not committed: household or building owner for private installation; employers for workplace assets; public or philanthropic support where affordability prevents access. Confirm ownership and recurrent payer locally.

    Fairness and risks

    Check water-fetching and cleaning labour, often borne unequally; provide accessible height and lids; do not call it a vaccine, meat or dairy refrigerator. No refrigerant or direct electrical load in the simple device; firing and replacement still have embodied impacts.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Bankass and Samanko, Mali, 2017 field phase; 2021 report. Household pot-in-pot and pot-in-dish configurations tested. Device count not reported in accessible summary Clay pot coolers: Mali report 2016–2021 (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Soroti, Uganda, 2019. Clay-pot/dish unit assembled using local household items. One named household example MIT D-Lab: dissemination in rural Uganda (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study Sensors and vegetable-quality tests supported storage cooling; dissemination and user experiences were documented separately. Clay pot coolers: Mali report 2016–2021 (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Implementer documented household assembly and use in Soroti; no independent impact evaluation is claimed. MIT D-Lab: dissemination in rural Uganda (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Translate pot sizes, local pottery, vegetable choice and water availability; do not transfer dry-season Mali performance to humid Asian monsoons.

    Other sources

    • MIT D-Lab/World Vegetable Center evaluation, Mali (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Storage cooling and adoption have been observed.

    Inferred: Could reduce some produce losses where the microclimate and use suit it.

    Uncertain: Local installed price, regular water demand and long-term household income effects are not established here.

    Brick-and-wet-sand zero-energy produce chamberPassive coolingDry heatReported, not evaluatedEvaporation from wetted porous brick walls and sand removes heat from a shaded storage enclosure.

    How it works

    Evaporation from wetted porous brick walls and sand removes heat from a shaded storage enclosure. The higher interior humidity helps limit produce water loss; this is not space cooling for workers.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry heat. A dry ambient atmosphere, shade and air movement are needed; high humidity restricts evaporation.

    What it has done

    • reported The project installed monitoring sensors, but a numeric chamber-temperature reduction is not reported on the reviewed programme page. Gujarat, India, 2019–2020 pilot. Three constructed chambers. Limits: Capacity is not cooling effectiveness; no human-health outcome. MIT D-Lab: brick cooling chambers (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Design matches crate size and storage needs; land, shade, water, drainage and an operating custodian are agreed.

    What could stop it

    Land access, water shortages, unsuitable humidity, blocked drainage or produce handling that defeats cooling.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal or inferred price supplied.

    Upkeep

    Named operators wet sand/brick, keep the cover shaded and clean produce contact areas; service interval and lifetime not specified.

    Who acts

    Farmers’ organisations and agriculture agencies, Community and civil society groups, Employers and businesses, Water authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed, not committed: household or building owner for private installation; employers for workplace assets; public or philanthropic support where affordability prevents access. Confirm ownership and recurrent payer locally.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess who controls communal storage, vendor fees, access for women farmers, reachable loading height and hygiene; allocate replenishment labour. No refrigerant in passive construction; water and material burdens remain.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Mandavav, Goriya and Santrampur, Gujarat, India, October 2019. Pilot construction with CInI and farmer participation. Three chambers; design capacity about 400 kg produce each MIT D-Lab: piloting in western India (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Soroti, Uganda, 2019. TEWDI/AEST chamber built for produce storage. One documented chamber MIT D-Lab: dissemination in rural Uganda (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Reported, not evaluated Implementer documented construction, equipment and locations, not a completed independent evaluation. MIT D-Lab: piloting in western India (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Inferred: Potentially useful for small-market supply chains without reliable electricity.

    Wetted terracotta screen or water-wall modulePassive coolingDry heatReported, not evaluatedAir passing a wetted porous ceramic surface can lose sensible heat as water evaporates; the screen may also shade the opening.

    How it works

    Air passing a wetted porous ceramic surface can lose sensible heat as water evaporates; the screen may also shade the opening. Gravity-fed operation is passive, but pumped recirculation is better counted as a low-energy hybrid.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry heat. Dry incoming air creates more evaporative potential; direct evaporation adds moisture and cannot safely be assumed suitable for hot-humid interiors.

    What it has done

    • reported The developer describes evaporative/natural-ventilation operation but publishes no verified thermal effect or comparative test on the reviewed project page. Lucknow, India, 2018. One festival installation. Limits: Vendor report; no quantified performance or health claim retained. CoolAnt: Lucknow IISF installation (opens in a new tab) ↗

    What makes it work

    Air can pass the wetted surface, replenishment and drainage are designed, and seasonal humidity is checked.

    What could stop it

    Dust/scaling, poor water quality, insufficient airflow, pump failure, wet structural details or unsuitable humidity.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal or inferred price supplied.

    Upkeep

    Operator would ideally maintain wetted surfaces, water circuit and safe drainage; no published universal lifespan or cleaning interval verified.

    Who acts

    Employers and businesses, City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Water authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed, not committed: household or building owner for private installation; employers for workplace assets; public or philanthropic support where affordability prevents access. Confirm ownership and recurrent payer locally.

    Fairness and risks

    Treat water quality, standing-water control, slipping, ceramic breakage and cleaning access as design checks. Identify who performs upkeep, including gendered labour; check renters’ permissions. Vendor statements about air purification or cooling magnitude are not verified.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated IISF, Lucknow, India, 2018. Beehive modular installation. One temporary demonstration; surface area not reported CoolAnt: Lucknow IISF installation (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test New Delhi, India, Not reported. Binary terracotta facade prototype. One prototype; surface area not reported CoolAnt: Binary facade prototype, New Delhi (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Reported, not evaluated CoolAnt describes a built demonstration using terracotta modules. CoolAnt: Lucknow IISF installation (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Developer describes the New Delhi Binary installation as a facade prototype; independent cooling verification was not found. CoolAnt: Binary facade prototype, New Delhi (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Require local wet-bulb/climate testing, measured outlet and occupied-zone conditions and a recorded pump load before procurement.

    Other sources

    • MIT D-Lab: piloting in western India (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known: Built/prototype installations are documented by the developer.
