    AC sizing, commissioning and operational controlsActive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataCommissioning checks whether capacity, airflow, refrigerant charge, schedules and controls meet the intended load and occupancy.

    How it works

    Commissioning checks whether capacity, airflow, refrigerant charge, schedules and controls meet the intended load and occupancy. It restores or verifies performance rather than creating cooling by itself.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Context-dependent system practice for both climates; hot-humid designs would ideally verify latent loads, outdoor air and condensate, not only room dry-bulb temperature.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Official cases report energy improvements following recommissioning plus other building measures; no isolated room-AC savings percentage transferred. US school case examples, Dates not reported on reviewed guidance page. Two named schools. Limits: Multiple interventions; US school budgets/climates do not establish Asian household savings. US DOE HVAC commissioning (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Savings depend on starting faults and corrected operation; no universal watt or percentage value.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Depends on actual equipment, refrigerant and electricity supply; no whole-lifecycle zero-emission claim.

    In a power cut

    Operational checking depends on functioning equipment; improved commissioning does not provide outage backup.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Electricity use, outdoor heat rejection and/or refrigerant loss may reinforce the cooling loop. What helps: Reduce avoidable load; choose appropriate climate/efficiency, reliable maintenance and low-impact supply.

    For the poorest

    Do not infer affordability from efficiency; obtain installed price, tariff, use hours and maintenance arrangements. Tenant and informal-worker access needs separate design.

    What makes it work

    Qualified technician/facility operator, documented target conditions, functioning sensors and authority/budget to correct faults.

    What could stop it

    Oversizing, mismatched components, poor records, inaccessible equipment, split landlord/tenant incentives and no follow-up repair budget.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed as a comparable installed local price in reviewed sources.

    Upkeep

    Assign a qualified operator/service provider; follow current manufacturer and local safety requirements. No universal service life or frequency established.

    Who acts

    National governments, International bodies, Employers and businesses, Utilities and energy regulators, City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: owner/employer/public-facility budget; targeted public support or grants where people cannot afford service. No funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Screen whether control changes restrict access or overrule vulnerable users. Maintain ventilation and electrical/refrigerant safety; no blanket temperature setpoint prescribed.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Chesterfield, Missouri, United States, Date not reported. Recommissioning and building improvements reported; transferable process lesson. Parkway West High School US DOE HVAC commissioning (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Los Angeles, California, United States, Date not reported. Audit/recommissioning and other energy measures reported; no isolated AC effect. Santee Education Complex US DOE HVAC commissioning (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Official guidance or data DOE describes commissioning and named school case examples. US DOE HVAC commissioning (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Transition to purpose-designed low-GWP room ACActive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataSelecting purpose-designed low-GWP refrigerant equipment reduces the climate consequence of refrigerant leakage relative to high-GWP alternatives.

    How it works

    Selecting purpose-designed low-GWP refrigerant equipment reduces the climate consequence of refrigerant leakage relative to high-GWP alternatives. Refrigerant choice alone does not establish cooling or electricity savings.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both climates if the certified equipment is rated for local temperature/humidity, charge limits and installation conditions; this is a procurement/transition measure, not an independent thermal mechanism.

    What it has done

    • reported R290 100-year GWP is 0.02 under the cited IPCC AR6 table; this is a gas metric, not measured programme emissions avoided. Global physical metric, GIZ 2022 table citing IPCC AR6. Not a field sample. Limits: Do not mix with older assessment GWP values or infer whole-system zero emissions. GIZ WE4F technical guidelines, AR6 refrigerant table (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Low GWP does not imply low electricity consumption; obtain certified equipment-specific seasonal performance.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Specific R290 metric; compare efficiency, leakage and electricity separately. R290 is not a zero-footprint product.

    In a power cut

    Electrical components need a dependable supply; autonomy and backup duration are not established.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Electricity use, outdoor heat rejection and/or refrigerant loss may reinforce the cooling loop. What helps: Reduce avoidable load; choose appropriate climate/efficiency, reliable maintenance and low-impact supply.

    For the poorest

    Do not infer affordability from efficiency; obtain installed price, tariff, use hours and maintenance arrangements. Tenant and informal-worker access needs separate design.

    What makes it work

    Compliant purpose-designed equipment, trained installers, flammability safety assessment and service network.

    What could stop it

    Unsafe drop-in substitution, absent local approval/service skills, unsuitable charge/room arrangements and upfront financing.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed as a comparable installed local price in reviewed sources.

    Upkeep

    Assign a qualified operator/service provider; follow current manufacturer and local safety requirements. No universal service life or frequency established.

    Who acts

    National governments, International bodies, Employers and businesses, Utilities and energy regulators, City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: owner/employer/public-facility budget; targeted public support or grants where people cannot afford service. No funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    R290 is flammable; do not offer DIY conversions or charging instructions. Screen access to safe installation, maintenance and affordable electricity.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated India, 2025 guide; historical commercial production. Godrej R290 split AC production documented. Over one million units sold reported by guide, not independently verified installation count GIZ/UBA R290 Split AC Resource Guide v 2.02 (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Accra, Takoradi, Kumasi and Tamale, Ghana, 2024. R290 ACs/tools provided for adoption and safe-service training. Four technical centres GIZ/EPA Ghana R290 technician and equipment programme (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Official guidance or data Resource guide documents commercially produced R290 ACs and installation/safety requirements. GIZ/UBA R290 Split AC Resource Guide v 2.02 (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated R290 ACs and tools distributed to four Ghana technical centres with technician training. GIZ/EPA Ghana R290 technician and equipment programme (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Kigali phases down HFC production and consumption on differentiated country timelines. It does not establish that existing equipment is already low-GWP. UNEP Ozone Secretariat overview (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Leak prevention, refrigerant recovery and end-of-life managementActive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyLeak detection/repair helps retain intended refrigerant charge.

    How it works

    Leak detection/repair helps retain intended refrigerant charge. Recovery captures gas during servicing/decommissioning; subsequent reuse, reclamation or destruction requires a managed chain. This is an enabling service, not a standalone cooler.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Context-dependent practice for both climates; training, equipment, refrigerant identification and safe storage/disposal would ideally match the actual gases.

    • reported Hands-on technician training documented; no measured avoided leakage or energy saving attributed. Pusa, New Delhi, India, 21–25 October 2024. 24 master trainers from 12 ITIs. Limits: Training attendance is not evidence gas was recovered or emissions were avoided. GIZ India good service practice training (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Correct charge/servicing can preserve performance; recovery/destruction equipment also consumes energy. No generic net value verified.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Refrigerants differ: avoided CO2e requires measured captured mass, gas identity, baseline leakage, treatment outcome and a stated GWP assessment. No avoided tonnage calculated.

    In a power cut

    Tools/collection infrastructure may require power; service does not provide cooling during an outage.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Electricity use, outdoor heat rejection and/or refrigerant loss may reinforce the cooling loop. What helps: Reduce avoidable load; choose appropriate climate/efficiency, reliable maintenance and low-impact supply.

    Do not infer affordability from efficiency; obtain installed price, tariff, use hours and maintenance arrangements. Tenant and informal-worker access needs separate design.

    Qualified technicians, correct tools/cylinders, finance for collection, traceability and permitted downstream treatment.

    What could stop it

    Integrated dehumidification with separate sensible coolingActive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyA dedicated subsystem removes moisture while another handles sensible heat.

    How it works

    A dedicated subsystem removes moisture while another handles sensible heat. This can avoid using excessive sensible cooling merely to control humidity; dehumidification requires energy and standalone units reject heat.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Especially relevant to hot-humid buildings with latent loads; in dry conditions extra dehumidification may be unnecessary. Capacity, ventilation and controls determine benefit.

    What it has done

    • measured Singapore crossover study reported radiant/all-air energy comparison, but it does not isolate dehumidification energy savings; no isolated percentage attributed here. Singapore, 2024 publication; measurement calendar dates not in abstract. 78 participants across five groups. Limits: Published abstract only; integrated-system comparison does not isolate latent-removal saving or establish medical heat protection. Li et al., Singapore radiant/all-air crossover study (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Include chiller/compressor, ventilation, desiccant regeneration if present, pumps and controls. No isolated dehumidification watts/kWh verified.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Actual chiller/AC refrigerant and heat source depend on design; no low GWP assumed from decoupling.

    In a power cut

    Electrical components need a dependable supply; autonomy and backup duration are not established.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Electricity use, outdoor heat rejection and/or refrigerant loss may reinforce the cooling loop. What helps: Reduce avoidable load; choose appropriate climate/efficiency, reliable maintenance and low-impact supply.

    For the poorest

    Do not infer affordability from efficiency; obtain installed price, tariff, use hours and maintenance arrangements. Tenant and informal-worker access needs separate design.

    What makes it work

    Measuredlatent/sensible loads, condensationcontrol, ventilation, condensatedrainage and coordinatedsystem operation.

    What could stop it

    Poorcontrol, leakyenvelopes, undersizedmoistureremoval, maintenanceburden, highcapitalcost and inadequate drainage.

    Rough cost

    Not publicly disclosed as a comparable installed local price in reviewed sources.

    Upkeep

    Assign a qualified operator/service provider; follow current manufacturer and local safety requirements. No universal service life or frequency established.

    Who acts

    Employers and businesses, Utilities and energy regulators, City and local governments, Community and civil society groups, Schools and education authorities, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: owner/employer/public-facility budget; targeted public support or grants where people cannot afford service. No funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Screen moisture/mould risks, access to skilled operators and high upfront cost. A portable dehumidifier in a closed room is not free cooling and may warm the air.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated United World College, Singapore, 2014–2018 project. Dedicated ventilation/dehumidification combined with sensible cooling. One built 3for2 demonstrator ETH/Singapore 3for2 demonstrator (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Bahadurgarh, India, October 2020 field phase;2021 report. Prototype room AC handled latent loads separately; not a mass-market deployment. One Transaera/Haier prototype among finalists RMI Global Cooling Prize testing report (opens in a new tab) ↗

    District cooling networksActive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataA central plant supplies chilled water through insulated pipes to several buildings.

    How it works

    A central plant supplies chilled water through insulated pipes to several buildings. Sharing production and different load profiles can change plant sizing and operation; distribution is distinct from storage.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both conditionally: equipment, humidity treatment, heat rejection and service arrangements would be worth designing for the local load.

    What it has done

    • reported Operator states 30% lower energy use than traditional AC, but publishes no measurement method or matched baseline on this page. GIFT City, Gujarat, India, Undated live page checked 2026-10-27. Network; sample and monitoring period not stated. Limits: Implementer claim only; not an independently measured saving. Do not use for local benefit calculations. GIFT City official district-cooling description (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Efficiency is system-specific; include distribution pumps, building air-side equipment and heat rejection, not only rated chiller COP.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    The historical GIFT engineering account specifies R134a. This does not make district cooling inherently low-GWP; current plant inventory and leakage require checking.

    In a power cut

    Fans, pumps, controls and/or compressors need a reliable electricity supply. Backup duration is not verified.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Expanded cooling can increase energy demand, refrigerant emissions and heat rejection. What helps: Reduce cooling load first, select and maintain efficient systems, verify refrigerant management and affordable access.

    For the poorest

    No verified purchase/running-cost share of poor-household income. Public subsidy, aggregation or public-service provision would require explicit design.

    What makes it work

    Building loads and connection timing justify pipes; rights of way, contracts and plant/building interfaces are resolved.

    What could stop it

    Low load density, uncertain connection schedules, disruptive excavation, insufficient return-water temperature difference and inappropriate tariffs are screening issues.

    Rough cost

    Project-specific installed and operating prices not publicly disclosed in the reviewed sources. No universal price or affordability claim inferred.

    Upkeep

    Assign qualified operators, water/refrigerant checks, controls maintenance and funded renewal. Published transferable service life and maintenance frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Utilities and energy regulators, Employers and businesses, Development banks, donors and climate funds, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: contracted building owners/public institutions pay capital or service charges; providers or investors may finance assets. No funding commitment inferred.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess who can connect, who pays, tariff transparency, continuity for essential services, tenant protections, disability-accessible cooled spaces and gendered exposure. Building-level cooling does not automatically protect outdoor workers or neighbouring households. Check cooling-tower water demand and treatment, construction disruption, connection charges, monopoly/service-contract terms and access for unconnected settlements.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated GIFT City, Gujarat, India, Live page checked 2026-10-27; source undated. Current operator-listed network, not the full planned buildout. Operational capacity stated 10,000 TR; full planned capacity separate GIFT City official district-cooling description (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Marina Bay, Singapore, 2026-08-14. Operating network; future expansions remain proposed/planned. 28 connected buildings reported SP Group Marina Bay operating network and expansion update (opens in a new tab) ↗

    • Official guidance or data Official guide describes planning and operation of shared networks. BEE district-cooling guidance report (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated GIFT operator identifies an operational district-cooling system. GIFT City official district-cooling description (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated SP reports ongoing Marina Bay operation and distinguishes future connections. SP Group Marina Bay operating network and expansion update (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Transfer the mechanism, not a published percentage. Reassess climate, occupancy, water, electricity mix, supplier capacity and affordable access.

    Cooling as a Service contractsActive coolingDry and humid heatReported, not evaluatedUsers buy a cooling service while a provider owns and operates equipment.

    How it works

    Users buy a cooling service while a provider owns and operates equipment. This changes finance, maintenance responsibility and incentives; it creates no separate physical cooling effect.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both as a delivery model; climate suitability belongs to the contracted equipment and humidity/comfort specification, not the financing contract.

    What it has done

    • reported Provider describes payment per service rather than customer ownership of the cooling equipment; no contract-level independent thermal or health effect verified. Singapore/India provider portfolio, Undated page checked 2026-10-27. Published commercial service model; no evaluation sample. Limits: A service fee replaces some capital/operating obligations; it is not free cooling or proof of savings. Kaer published cooling-as-a-service model (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Energy use belongs to the installed plant. The contract can influence incentives but is not itself a kWh-saving device.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    The contract has no refrigerant. Require disclosure of equipment refrigerants, leakage and electricity emissions; provider carbon-neutral language is not an independent lifecycle finding.

    In a power cut

    Fans, pumps, controls and/or compressors need a reliable electricity supply. Backup duration is not verified.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Expanded cooling can increase energy demand, refrigerant emissions and heat rejection. What helps: Reduce cooling load first, select and maintain efficient systems, verify refrigerant management and affordable access.

    For the poorest

    Cases are institutional/commercial. No evidence collected that the poorest households qualify or face affordable service fees; aggregated public procurement or subsidies are possibilities, not verified routes.

    What makes it work

    Service levels, metering, data access, escalation, performance verification, minimum payments and failure/exit arrangements are enforceable.

    What could stop it

    Credit/scale requirements may exclude small or informal customers; assess procurement ability, contract lock-in and risk allocation.

    Rough cost

    Public per-RTH tariff, total contract cost, minimum-offtake charges and termination liabilities not verified. Provider no-capex language is contract-specific, not zero lifetime cost.

    Upkeep

    The published Kaer model assigns equipment operation, maintenance and repair to the provider; verify the actual signed contract and renewal/end-of-term obligations.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Utilities and energy regulators, Employers and businesses, Development banks, donors and climate funds, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Published cases describe building customers paying for cooling service while the provider finances/operates equipment. Actual tariffs are not disclosed.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess who can connect, who pays, tariff transparency, continuity for essential services, tenant protections, disability-accessible cooled spaces and gendered exposure. Building-level cooling does not automatically protect outdoor workers or neighbouring households.

    Ice thermal storage for coolingActive coolingDry and humid heatReported, not evaluatedA chiller freezes water when electricity is available or cheaper; melting ice later supplies cooling.

    How it works

    A chiller freezes water when electricity is available or cheaper; melting ice later supplies cooling. Latent storage shifts production in time and is distinct from a chilled-water tank.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both conditionally: equipment, humidity treatment, heat rejection and service arrangements would be worth designing for the local load.

    What it has done

    • reported Existing Marina Bay thermal-storage tanks were reported to contribute up to 11 MW of electrical load-curtailment capacity. Marina Bay, Singapore, 2022-08-29. Five thermal-storage tanks in the operating network. Limits: Capacity, not MWh saved. The separate George Street pilot was only announced; its original delivery date was superseded by later planning. EMA/SP thermal-storage pilot announcement and existing tank demand response (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Charging a colder ice-making cycle can add electricity use; off-peak cost or demand savings are not proof of lower total energy.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Water/ice is the storage medium, not the generating chiller refrigerant. Refrigerant and GWP would be worth obtaining from the actual charging plant; not disclosed for these examples.

    In a power cut

    Stored cooling may reduce compressor operation temporarily, but distribution pumps, fans and controls still need power. No outage duration verified.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Expanded cooling can increase energy demand, refrigerant emissions and heat rejection. What helps: Reduce cooling load first, select and maintain efficient systems, verify refrigerant management and affordable access.

    Stratified chilled-water thermal storageActive coolingDry and humid heatReported, not evaluatedA tank stores cold water below warmer water; careful inlets limit mixing.

    How it works

    A tank stores cold water below warmer water; careful inlets limit mixing. It supplies cooling later using sensible temperature differences rather than freezing water.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both conditionally: equipment, humidity treatment, heat rejection and service arrangements would be worth designing for the local load.

    What it has done

    • measured A laboratory half-cycle figure of merit was approximately 0.9 at the specified flow. India; exact experimental location not stated in accessed section, 2025 publication. 150-litre tank with 0.5 TR chiller; 100 L/hour test case. Limits: Small rig thermal-stratification metric, not annual energy saving or occupied-building cooling efficacy. Heat-transfer analysis of stratified chilled-water storage tank (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Storage shifts chiller operating time; thermal losses and pumps matter. Warmer storage temperatures can avoid the ice-making temperature requirement, but local total-energy savings would be worth measuring.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Storage water itself needs no refrigerant. The historical GIFT generating chiller used R134a; the sourced GWP basis below does not establish the current plant inventory or a factor for every district plant.

    In a power cut

    Fans, pumps, controls and/or compressors need a reliable electricity supply. Backup duration is not verified.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Expanded cooling can increase energy demand, refrigerant emissions and heat rejection. What helps: Reduce cooling load first, select and maintain efficient systems, verify refrigerant management and affordable access.

    For the poorest

    No verified purchase/running-cost share of poor-household income. Public subsidy, aggregation or public-service provision would require explicit design.

    What makes it work

    Demand, load profiles, operating capability and payment responsibilities are established before procurement.

    What could stop it

    Screen for unsuitable demand, weak service contracts, unreliable utilities, capital constraints and lack of maintenance capability.

    Rough cost

    Project-specific installed and operating prices not publicly disclosed in the reviewed sources. No universal price or affordability claim inferred.

    Upkeep

    Assign qualified operators, water/refrigerant checks, controls maintenance and funded renewal. Published transferable service life and maintenance frequency not verified.

    Who acts

    City and local governments, Utilities and energy regulators, Employers and businesses, Development banks, donors and climate funds, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: contracted building owners/public institutions pay capital or service charges; providers or investors may finance assets. No funding commitment inferred.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess who can connect, who pays, tariff transparency, continuity for essential services, tenant protections, disability-accessible cooled spaces and gendered exposure. Building-level cooling does not automatically protect outdoor workers or neighbouring households. Tank space, insulation, water quality and pipe condensation need design. Distinguish closed-loop storage water from cooling-tower water consumption.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated GIFT City, Gujarat, India, Phase1 operational2015; engineering report2017/reprint2018. Constructed stratified-water storage; planned whole-city savings are not measured. 10,000 TR-hour tank reported GIFT City engineer: district cooling and stratified water tank (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Marina Bay, Singapore, 2019-07-26 report. Reported chilled-water storage combined with an electrical-battery pilot. Thermal storage system; water-tank capacity not specified on page SP Group chilled-water/lithium-battery pilot report (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    Solar-thermal absorption coolingActive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataSolar collectors supply heat to drive an absorption refrigeration cycle instead of a mechanical compressor.

    How it works

    Solar collectors supply heat to drive an absorption refrigeration cycle instead of a mechanical compressor. Pumps, fans, heat rejection and sometimes backup heat still need energy.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both conditionally: solar resource, heat-rejection design and sensible/latent loads control suitability. Hot-humid settings need dehumidification capacity and effective heat rejection; dry climates still need water-aware design.

    What it has done

    • reported Implementer reports 30% higher efficiency across four demonstration projects, without defining a common metric and matched baseline in the slides. Four sites, Jordan, 2018 conference report. Four operating demonstration sites. Limits: Not adopted as a transferable performance estimate; no independent evaluation or health outcome. GIZ Proklima: Solar Cooling for Industry and Commerce, Jordan (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Solar heat supplies part of the refrigeration input; electrical pumps/fans and any backup heater remain. Thermal COP and electrical COP use different denominators.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Jordan systems use water refrigerant with lithium-bromide absorbent. No numeric water GWP100 assigned; assess auxiliaries, backup heat and heat rejection.

    In a power cut

    Auxiliary pumps, controls and fans require electricity; cloudy periods/night cooling require designed thermal storage or backup. No autonomous duration verified.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Expanded cooling can increase energy demand, refrigerant emissions and heat rejection. What helps: Reduce cooling load first, select and maintain efficient systems, verify refrigerant management and affordable access.

    Solar-direct-drive vaccine refrigerationActive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataPV electricity runs a refrigeration compressor directly; integrated cold storage maintains temperature between sunny periods.

    How it works

    PV electricity runs a refrigeration compressor directly; integrated cold storage maintains temperature between sunny periods. The system is active refrigeration even when electrical batteries are absent.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both if the particular system is rated and site-assessed. UNICEF specifies hot-zone qualification at +43°C and a solar reference condition; cloudy/humid locations still need site-specific solar assessment.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance UNICEF describes WHO-PQS hot-zone performance requirements at +43°C with a solar radiation reference of 3.5 kWh/m²/day. WHO-PQS qualification conditions; global procurement, September 2026 update. System classes, not a field sample. Limits: Solar irradiation is not refrigerator electricity consumption; no generic holdover or clinical benefit inferred. UNICEF solar-powered refrigeration systems pricing and specifications (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Solar electricity drives compressor cooling. UNICEF distinguishes battery-free SDD systems; no generic refrigerator watts or kWh/day extracted.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No generic refrigerant or lifecycle emissions assigned; connected equipment and electricity source would be worth identifying.

    In a power cut

    Documented SDD systems do not require grid electricity or electrical batteries for the refrigeration cycle; commissioning would ideally match solar resources and required service.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Enabling more electrically powered cooling may increase demand and waste heat. What helps: Combine need-based cooling, efficient equipment, clean supply, maintenance and safe refrigerant management.

    For the poorest

    Not established. Procurement, subsidy or a service fee does not demonstrate affordability for the poorest.

    What makes it work

    Procurement, installation, solar siting, temperature monitoring, staff training and service support fit the immunization programme. Follow current equipment-specific WHO/national requirements.

    What could stop it

    Screen capital, operating finance, maintenance skills, spares, land/roof permissions, procurement and responsible operation.

    Rough cost

    • Upfront: 2944–4332 USD per complete solar refrigeration system; Dulas refrigerator-category range, multiple models

    Prices from 2026. UNICEF 2026 range in September 2026 update, FCA containerized sea-shipment basis. Not local installed cost, not one model quote; import, freight, installation and service expenses are not inferred. UNICEF Solar-powered refrigerator systems pricing 2022–2026 (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Upkeep

    Assign commissioning, monitoring, maintenance, spares and replacement responsibilities; no universal lifespan or inspection interval verified.

    Who acts

    Health authorities, Utilities and energy regulators, Development banks, donors and climate funds, International bodies. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: service owner, public budget or grant-supported capital plus an identified operating payer. No named commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Check access for women, low-income and disabled users; assign maintenance labour and affordable access. Do not infer inclusion from installed equipment.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Bongaigaon/Brahmaputra boat-clinic setting, Assam, India, Reported 17 October 2024. Solar-direct-drive refrigeration supports immunization outreach. Solar unit aboard boat clinic; individual unit capacity not reported UNICEF Akha boat clinic solar direct-drive refrigeration (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Ceegbah clinic, Grand Bassa County, Liberia, Installed September 2022; reported April 2023. Refrigerator stores vaccines locally rather than requiring every collection trip to the county depot. One named clinic installation UNICEF Ceegbah clinic solar direct-drive refrigerator (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Validated cold transport: freeze-preventive vaccine carriersActive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyInsulation and a thermal-buffer liner separate vaccines from frozen packs, reducing accidental freezing while maintaining a transport cold chain.

    How it works

    Insulation and a thermal-buffer liner separate vaccines from frozen packs, reducing accidental freezing while maintaining a transport cold chain. Upstream ice-pack freezing uses active refrigeration; the carrier itself is passive.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both, subject to site-specific design. System measures have no intrinsic temperature reduction; equipment would ideally be rated for actual ambient heat/humidity and the service it supports.

    What it has done

    • measured Carriers avoided temperatures below 0°C for more than 99%of monitored time, except one cold-ambient site below the minimum rated testing temperature. Eastern Nepal health posts, Trials 2018–19; paper 2022. Three carrier designs,24 healthposts. Limits: Not proof of safe handling under all heat conditions. Temperature guidance is product/vaccine specific; no general storage range prescribed here. Kumar et al., freeze-preventive vaccine carriers in Nepal (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Carrier has no onboard compressor; frozen packs require an upstream freezer. The chain, rather than the insulated box alone, has an energy requirement.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No refrigerant in the passive carrier; upstream freezer refrigerant and electricity affect the whole-chain footprint.

    In a power cut

    Transport segment can operate without onboard grid power; upstream pack preparation and temperature monitoring would ideally remain functional.

    The cooling-trap risk

    More transport capacity can increase upstream freezing and logistics loads. What helps: Validate packout and routes, avoid unnecessary chilling and procure efficient upstream equipment.

    For the poorest

    Not established. Procurement, subsidy or a service fee does not demonstrate affordability for the poorest.

    What makes it work

    Carrier, pack preparation, route duration, ambient envelope and training are validated together under current guidance.

    What could stop it

    Screen capital, operating finance, maintenance skills, spares, land/roof permissions, procurement and responsible operation.

    Rough cost

    Not verified as separable local installed, operating and upkeep costs in reviewed sources. No global price inferred.

    Upkeep

    Assign commissioning, monitoring, maintenance, spares and replacement responsibilities; no universal lifespan or inspection interval verified.

    Who acts

    Health authorities, International bodies, Development banks, donors and climate funds. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: service owner, public budget or grant-supported capital plus an identified operating payer. No named commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Study users requested smaller/lighter carriers; transport burden matters for outreach workers. Screen access, carrying burden and routes for women and disabled staff rather than assuming a heavier box improves delivery.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Sunsari district plains, eastern Nepal, Simulated 2018/2019; actual-useNovember–December 2019. Freeze-preventive carriers carried to outreach sessions. Part of 24 healthposts across two districts; district allocation not extracted PATH field evaluation of freeze-preventive vaccine carriers (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Dhankuta district hills, eastern Nepal, Same 2018–19 evaluation. Different transport/ambient context within same study, not an independent second country replication. Part of 24 healthposts across two districts PATH field evaluation of freeze-preventive vaccine carriers (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer mechanisms rather than copying equipment sizes, tariffs or reported outcomes.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Off-grid and hybrid water-service examples are documented in South Asia.

    Inferred: Maintaining accessible water supports heat preparedness and essential services.

    Uncertain: Heat-specific health effects, sustainable abstraction, actual outage performance, local installed/operating costs and poorest-user affordability remain unverified.

    Demand response and scheduled flexible loads to relieve heat-period peaksActive coolingDry and humid heatReported, not evaluatedOperators shift flexible electricity use away from constrained hours or reward reductions, preserving grid headroom.

    How it works

    Operators shift flexible electricity use away from constrained hours or reward reductions, preserving grid headroom. This is an operating system, not a cooling device; essential cooling would ideally remain protected.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both, subject to site-specific design. System measures have no intrinsic temperature reduction; equipment would ideally be rated for actual ambient heat/humidity and the service it supports.

    What it has done

    • reported Utility reports 345 kWshifted for 3 hours daily in a 23-day February 2024 trial, with more than 23,000 kWhshifted across the trial. BMC-Bhandup, Mumbai, India, February 2024; publishedMarch 2024. One named pumping-station pilot,23 days. Limits: Load shifting is not energy saving. Provider-reported result; no independent metered verification or resulting heat-health benefit extracted. Tata Power/MCGM pumping demand flexibility pilot (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • reported Project reports 28.8 MWof new flexible-demand reductions by end-summer 2022. California, UnitedStates, Through summer 2022; report 2024. More than 41,000 newcustomers enrolled. Limits: MWis power, not energy. Provider-authored project summary, not independent evaluation. CEC/OhmConnect Building Resiliency from Within final-project summary (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Mumbai reports a 345 kWloadshift, not a device wattage or energy-efficiency gain; California reports 28.8 MWflexible-demand capacity. No generic consumption assigned.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No refrigerant inherent in demand response. Emissions depend on what load moves, timing and marginal generation; carbon savings not assumed from time shifting alone.

    In a power cut

    Requires grid coordination, reliable metering/communications and flexible loads; it is not backup power for an individual household.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Indiscriminate curtailment can remove cooling from people who need it; shifted demand may rebound later. What helps: Protect critical cooling and water service; use verified flexible loads and safe participation/override rules.

    For the poorest

    Not established. Procurement, subsidy or a service fee does not demonstrate affordability for the poorest.

    What makes it work

    Design matches actual service loads, users and local conditions.

    What could stop it

    Screen capital, operating finance, maintenance skills, spares, land/roof permissions, procurement and responsible operation.

    Rough cost

    Not verified as separable local installed, operating and upkeep costs in reviewed sources. No global price inferred.

    Upkeep

    Assign commissioning, monitoring, maintenance, spares and replacement responsibilities; no universal lifespan or inspection interval verified.

    Who acts

    Utilities and energy regulators, Water authorities, City and local governments, Employers and businesses, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: service owner, public budget or grant-supported capital plus an identified operating payer. No named commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Check access for women, low-income and disabled users; assign maintenance labour and affordable access. Do not infer inclusion from installed equipment.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Bhandup municipal water pumping, Mumbai, India, February 2024. Pumping moved towards solar/off-peak times. One 23-daypilot Tata Power/MCGM pumping demand flexibility pilot (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated California residential demand-response programme, UnitedStates, 2021–2022; report 2024. Transferable operating lesson, but tariff/telemetry/customer contexts differ substantially from Asia. More than 41,000 newcustomers reported CEC/OhmConnect Building Resiliency from Within final-project summary (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Reported, not evaluated Utility reports shifting municipal pumping demand in a February 2024 pilot. Tata Power/MCGM pumping demand flexibility pilot (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated CEC-hosted final-project summary reports residential demand-response enrollment and peak reduction; authored by provider. CEC/OhmConnect Building Resiliency from Within final-project summary (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer mechanisms rather than copying equipment sizes, tariffs or reported outcomes.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Specified Indian and US programmes report flexible demand delivery.

    Inferred: Flexible pumping and other noncritical loads can be coordinated to preserve cooling-related grid headroom.

    Uncertain: Independent event savings, rebound, marginal emissions, effects on vulnerable users and transfer costs require local verification.

    How it works

    Utilities and public agencies coordinate forecasts, maintenance, regional transfers, reserves and demand measures to meet heat-period electricity needs. It enables cooling continuity rather than directly cooling a place.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Both, subject to site-specific design. System measures have no intrinsic temperature reduction; equipment would ideally be rated for actual ambient heat/humidity and the service it supports.

    What it has done

NorthernRegion, India, 17 June 2024; release 18 June 2024. One regional event; not an impact evaluation.     A grid-level enabling measure; requires capable operators, coordination and resources. Does not substitute for local critical-load resilience.

    The cooling-trap risk

    PCM or ice-pack cooling vestActive coolingDry and humid heatSimulation or testCold or phase-changing packs absorb body heat through conduction; the cooling supply is finite and needs regenerating.

    How it works

    Cold or phase-changing packs absorb body heat through conduction; the cooling supply is finite and needs regenerating. The worn vest can have no motor, while its freezer/refrigerator or recharge chain uses energy.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Conductive cooling is less directly dependent on evaporation than wet garments, but pack temperature, mass, clothing and metabolic heat determine benefit.

    What it has done

    • measured The trial found lower skin temperature, while some oral-temperature/strain effects were limited to lighter work and heart-rate differences were not significant. No universal numerical body-temperature reduction retained. Isfahan study team, Iran; exact chamber site not stated in abstract, 2013 experiment; 2016 publication. 12 healthy male students; 30-minute treadmill trials at two speeds. Limits: Older small laboratory study. Not a clinical protection or full-shift field result. Dehghan et al.: PCM vest climatic-chamber trial (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • measured A newly designed vest intervention during rest reduced measured physiological/perceptual strain relative to control; hybrid components and break time prevent attribution to PCM alone. Hong Kong construction research; exact worksite not disclosed in abstract, 2018 publication. 14 construction workers; repeated cooling/control trials. Limits: Abstract-only; tympanic temperature is not rectal core temperature; no morbidity endpoint. Zhao et al.: cooling intervention in construction workers (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Worn PCM/ice pack need not draw electricity; recharge energy and any hybrid fans would be worth measuring separately.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No refrigerant circulates in the pack itself; upstream freezing equipment refrigerant, leakage and electricity emissions are not disclosed.

    In a power cut

    Protection lasts only while the pack retains useful cooling capacity; outage resilience depends on actual ice/pack inventory, not a generic promise.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Cooling can add electricity demand, charging/refrigeration needs and waste heat outside the protected zone. What helps: Reduce exposure and envelope heat gain, use appropriate efficient cooling, maintain access and test actual energy demand; do not substitute gadgets for work-rest protection.

    For the poorest

    Purchase and recurrent costs as a share of income were not published in reviewed sources. Do not infer affordability or free access. Assess transport, missed earnings and maintenance/charging costs.

    What makes it work

    Appropriate pack temperatures, safe skin contact, fit, recharge logistics and replacement packs are provided with rest and hydration.

    What could stop it

    Melted/warm packs, insufficient freezer capacity, mobility restriction, unsuitable PPE integration or work intensification that offsets benefit.

    Rough cost

    No verified installed/local lifecycle price in the opened sources; affordability adjectives in abstracts are not accepted as price evidence.

    Upkeep

    Operator would ideally inspect, clean and maintain the cooling equipment and its energy/coolant supply. Obtain manufacturer-specific safe-use and replacement instructions; published validated life and servicing interval not verified here.

    Who acts

    Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: employer for required occupational protection; facility/public authority for shared public cooling. Confirm recurrent budget and access arrangements; no funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess weight, skin discomfort/cold injury, cleaning and shared-vest hygiene. Fit would ideally include women and different body sizes; it is fairer when workers do not pay for employer protection. Wearing the vest does not by itself justify longer exposure.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Iran; exact chamber site not disclosed in abstract, 2013 test; 2016 publication. PCM laboratory test; lighter and heavier treadmill workloads. 12 healthy male students Dehghan et al.: PCM vest climatic-chamber trial (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Hong Kong, China, 2018 publication. Rest-break intervention with a newly designed cooling vest; not pure PCM isolation. 14 construction workers Zhao et al.: cooling intervention in construction workers (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test PCM vest tested in hot-dry chamber; mixed outcome evidence retained. Dehghan et al.: PCM vest climatic-chamber trial (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Field cooling intervention tested during rest between work bouts; not a programme evaluation. Zhao et al.: cooling intervention in construction workers (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Check actual sun, humidity, workload and clothing; Iranian laboratory and Hong Kong rest results cannot guarantee continuous field protection.

    Other sources

    • Chan et al.: hybrid vest during Hong Kong rest breaks (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Tetzlaff et al.: personal cooling-garment systematic review (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Small tests show context-dependent benefits and limitations.

    Inferred: Can supplement occupational controls when the recharge chain is reliable.

    Uncertain: Full-shift health benefit, independent lifecycle cost, inclusive sizing and performance during grid interruption are not verified.

    Related practical actions: Outdoor and hot workplaces

    Circulating-liquid personal cooling vestActive coolingDry and humid heatSimulation or testA pump circulates chilled liquid through garment tubing to carry heat from the body to an ice reservoir or chiller.

    How it works

    A pump circulates chilled liquid through garment tubing to carry heat from the body to an ice reservoir or chiller. Cooling duration depends on the reservoir or external plant, pump and battery.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Conductive liquid transfer can work despite humidity; practical performance depends on workload, clothing and temperature of the circulating coolant.

    What it has done

    • measured After the 60-minute walking test, rectal temperature was 37.6 ± 0.1 °C with the vest versus 37.9 ± 0.1 °C without it. NIOSH Japan laboratory; exact facility city not specified on abstract page, 2020 issue; test dates not disclosed in abstract. Eight men; 60 minutes at 3.0 km/h; 33 °C, 60% RH; impermeable protective suit. Limits: Small controlled walking trial; not full workshift or clinical outcome. Tokizawa et al.: liquid vest under protective clothing (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • measured A cooling garment reduced several physiological/perceptual strain indicators in actual construction work; corrupted temperature units in the PubMed abstract are not reproduced. India; field worksite not identified in abstract, 2018 online; 2019 issue. 29 healthy construction workers. Limits: Garment pumping architecture is described in the secondary review; primary abstract alone does not provide energy input or exact device specification. Ashtekar et al.: construction-worker cooling garment (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Pump input and refrigeration/ice-making are required but wattage and daily kWh were not verified. Physiological heat removal is not electrical consumption.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Water/coolant in garment tubing is not a vapour-compression refrigerant; the upstream chiller/freezer refrigerant and GWP remain unspecified.

    In a power cut

    A battery can power the pump briefly, but a reliable cold source is still needed; no backup autonomy is assumed.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Cooling can add electricity demand, charging/refrigeration needs and waste heat outside the protected zone. What helps: Reduce exposure and envelope heat gain, use appropriate efficient cooling, maintain access and test actual energy demand; do not substitute gadgets for work-rest protection.

    For the poorest

    Purchase and recurrent costs as a share of income were not published in reviewed sources. Do not infer affordability or free access. Assess transport, missed earnings and maintenance/charging costs.

    What makes it work

    Battery/pump and chilled reservoir are maintained, tubing stays intact, and mobility/PPE compatibility are demonstrated.

    What could stop it

    Empty ice supply, battery loss, leaks, hose entanglement, unsuitable water temperatures or inadequate work-rest rights.

    Rough cost

    No verified installed/local lifecycle price in the opened sources; affordability adjectives in abstracts are not accepted as price evidence.

    Upkeep

    Operator would ideally inspect, clean and maintain the cooling equipment and its energy/coolant supply. Obtain manufacturer-specific safe-use and replacement instructions; published validated life and servicing interval not verified here.

    Who acts

    Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: employer for required occupational protection; facility/public authority for shared public cooling. Confirm recurrent budget and access arrangements; no funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess weight, restricted movement, skin tolerance, cleaning and electrical/hose safety. Device failure is not the worker’s fault; inclusive fit and subsidised replenishment matter.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Japan; exact chamber location not stated on reviewed abstract page, 2020 publication. Controlled protective-clothing liquid-cooling test. Eight male participants Tokizawa et al.: liquid vest under protective clothing (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test India; exact worksite not disclosed in abstract, 2019 issue. Field cooling garment test; recirculating architecture corroborated by review. 29 construction workers Ashtekar et al.: construction-worker cooling garment (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test Independent occupational-health researchers tested a field-type liquid vest in a chamber. Tokizawa et al.: liquid vest under protective clothing (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test ICMR-associated field trial tested a personal cooling garment; not a vendor marketing claim. Ashtekar et al.: construction-worker cooling garment (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Protective-suit laboratory evidence cannot establish effectiveness for every informal outdoor occupation or a full hot shift.

    Other sources

    • Tetzlaff et al.: personal cooling-garment systematic review (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Short controlled and field tests document physiological effects.

    Inferred: May be useful where clothing blocks evaporation and trained operational support is available.

    Uncertain: Actual pump watts, recharge kWh, field downtime, full lifecycle cost and heat-illness reduction are not verified.

    Related practical actions: Outdoor and hot workplaces

    Wetted garments or towels, including fan-assisted clothingActive coolingDry and humid heatSimulation or testWetting cloth adds water that can evaporate and carry heat away; fans may increase air movement through the garment.

    How it works

    Wetting cloth adds water that can evaporate and carry heat away; fans may increase air movement through the garment. Results for a fan-assisted wetted shirt cannot fairly be attributed to a wet towel alone.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Evaporation is constrained by humidity and clothing permeability; performance cannot be extrapolated across all humid heat or impermeable PPE conditions.

    What it has done

    • measured Rectal-temperature rise was about 0.7 °C with wet shirt plus fan garment versus 1.3 °C in the no-fan dry control in both age groups. NIOSH Japan laboratory, 2023 publication; exact trial dates not specified. Eight young and eight older men; 60-minute intermittent walking, 200–230 W/m²; 37 °C, 50% RH. Limits: Not a towel-only result; no solar radiation, heavy full-shift work or common chronic-disease population. Tokizawa: wetted inner clothing with ventilation garment (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • measured Facial infrared temperature averaged 34.8 °C with wetted headgear versus 35.2 °C without it. Singapore construction site, June 2018; paper 2021. 30 completing workers; crossover across two weeks. Limits: Facial skin temperature is not core temperature. This is wetted textile headgear, not a powered cooling safety helmet. Wan, Jia and Goh: Singapore cooling-headgear field study (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Unpowered wet cloth has no operating electricity, but studied fan garments require batteries; water use and fan charge energy would be worth counting.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No refrigerant in an ordinary wetted garment; chilled-water/ice preparation and fan power can add upstream impacts.

    In a power cut

    Simple wet cloth is not grid-dependent; fan-assisted versions lose the tested air-movement component if battery supply fails.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Cooling can add electricity demand, charging/refrigeration needs and waste heat outside the protected zone. What helps: Reduce exposure and envelope heat gain, use appropriate efficient cooling, maintain access and test actual energy demand; do not substitute gadgets for work-rest protection.

    For the poorest

    Purchase and recurrent costs as a share of income were not published in reviewed sources. Do not infer affordability or free access. Assess transport, missed earnings and maintenance/charging costs.

    What makes it work

    Water, safe hygienic wetting, clothing compatibility and air movement are available; separate actual physiological monitoring from comfort ratings.

    What could stop it

    High humidity, insufficient evaporation, inability to rewet, skin problems, unsuitable electrical/chemical exposure or a garment blocking sweat transfer.

    Rough cost

    No verified installed/local lifecycle price in the opened sources; affordability adjectives in abstracts are not accepted as price evidence.

    Upkeep

    Operator would ideally inspect, clean and maintain the cooling equipment and its energy/coolant supply. Obtain manufacturer-specific safe-use and replacement instructions; published validated life and servicing interval not verified here.

    Who acts

    Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, Community and civil society groups, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: employer for required occupational protection; facility/public authority for shared public cooling. Confirm recurrent budget and access arrangements; no funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess wet-clothing acceptability and privacy, including women’s needs, chafing, hygiene, disability/dexterity and safety around electrical tasks. Singapore participants reported weight/neck strain and rewetting disruption; avoid interpreting cool skin as proof of safety.

    Where it has been tried

    • Simulation or test Japan; exact laboratory city not established in methods inspected, 2023 publication. Water-soaked inner shirt with fan-assisted garment. 16 male volunteers Tokizawa: wetted inner clothing with ventilation garment (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Singapore, June 2018; paper 2021. Wet cooling headgear field trial, with reported rewetting inconvenience and neck discomfort. 30 completing rebar/carpentry workers Wan, Jia and Goh: Singapore cooling-headgear field study (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test Independent occupational-health laboratory study tested combined wetting and fanned clothing. Tokizawa: wetted inner clothing with ventilation garment (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Academic field trial evaluated wetted commercial headgear and user experience. Wan, Jia and Goh: Singapore cooling-headgear field study (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Separate low-energy textile wetting from powered fan support; do not publish a universal wet-towel protocol or use these experiments as emergency treatment instructions.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Combined laboratory effects and one academic field headgear test are documented.

    Inferred: May supplement protected rest in settings where water and evaporation permit.

    Uncertain: Clinical benefit, safe use for all ages/illnesses, humid full-shift benefit and costs are not established.

    Mechanically cooled worker rest shelterActive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyA cooled rest enclosure reduces environmental heat exposure while workers stop exertion.

    How it works

    A cooled rest enclosure reduces environmental heat exposure while workers stop exertion. Its real protection is a service combining cooling, paid usable breaks, proximity, capacity, water and management.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Mechanical cooling can serve both when designed for sensible/latent loads, ventilation and occupational use; a fan-only shelter is a different physical configuration.

    What it has done

    • measured An independently studied construction site had air-conditioned rest areas within a wider heat-protection package. The study does not isolate an AC-shelter effect. Qatar construction site, Summer 2019. Construction-site workers within a larger occupational study; isolated-shelter comparison absent. Limits: No numeric shelter-only thermal/health effect extracted; programme package attribution is limited. ILO/University of Thessaly: occupational heat-strain study Qatar (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    AC and ventilation create a recurring electrical load; installed demand, usage profile and peak impact not disclosed in the reviewed case.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    AC refrigerant identity, charge and leakage are not disclosed; GWP cannot be assigned. Procure efficient appropriate equipment and qualified maintenance without DIY refrigerant advice.

    In a power cut

    Grid dependence is substantial unless a verified backup system is installed; no battery runtime or outage protection assumed.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Cooling can add electricity demand, charging/refrigeration needs and waste heat outside the protected zone. What helps: Reduce exposure and envelope heat gain, use appropriate efficient cooling, maintain access and test actual energy demand; do not substitute gadgets for work-rest protection.

    For the poorest

    Purchase and recurrent costs as a share of income were not published in reviewed sources. Do not infer affordability or free access. Assess transport, missed earnings and maintenance/charging costs.

    What makes it work

    Breaks are permitted and paid/usable, shelter is reachable, capacity is sufficient, maintenance and cooling power are reliable.

    What could stop it

    Piece-rate income pressure, distant shelters, crowding, unavailable seats, restricted access or power failure.

    Rough cost

    No verified installed/local lifecycle price in the opened sources; affordability adjectives in abstracts are not accepted as price evidence.

    Upkeep

    Operator would ideally inspect, clean and maintain the cooling equipment and its energy/coolant supply. Obtain manufacturer-specific safe-use and replacement instructions; published validated life and servicing interval not verified here.

    Who acts

    Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, City and local governments, Health authorities. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: employer for required occupational protection; facility/public authority for shared public cooling. Confirm recurrent budget and access arrangements; no funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Ensure subcontracted/informal workers, women and disabled people can enter safely. Cooling infrastructure cannot compensate for withheld rest or wages. Assess hot travel, infection-control/ventilation, nighttime crowding, condenser exhaust and displacement of public trading space.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Qatar construction site, Summer 2019. Air-conditioned rest spaces within a multi-measure programme. Site workforce reported above 4,000; study sampling not reproduced here ILO/University of Thessaly: occupational heat-strain study Qatar (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Measured in a study University-led field study documented a protection package including cooled rest spaces and identified crowded cooling-room concerns. ILO/University of Thessaly: occupational heat-strain study Qatar (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Singapore’s August 2026 enhancement recommends ventilated, insulated or cooled shade; recommendation does not prove installed AC shelters at every site. Singapore MOM: enhancements to heat-stress framework (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Qatar programme observations do not prove an identical result in humid Asian sites; local loads, rest patterns and access require verification.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: A field package with cooled rest areas is documented; Singapore provides current guidance.

    Inferred: A properly operated shelter can support recovery when workers can actually use it.

    Uncertain: Second verified built location, isolated shelter effectiveness, inclusive access and lifecycle operating cost remain uncertain.

    Public air-conditioned cooling centre or shared refugeActive coolingDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataA cooled shared indoor place temporarily reduces exposure for people without adequate cooling at home or work.

    How it works

    A cooled shared indoor place temporarily reduces exposure for people without adequate cooling at home or work. The intervention includes access, operating hours, outreach and onward support, not just an air conditioner.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Appropriately sized mechanical cooling can lower exposure in both; hot-humid climates also need latent-load/ventilation management and safe travel to the refuge.

    What it has done

    • measured Core temperature was 0.8 °C lower after the two-hour cooling period; the difference did not persist through the subsequent hours of renewed heat exposure. University of Ottawa, Canada, February 2019–April 2021 trials; 2023 paper. 40 adults aged 64–79; nine-hour simulated heatwave; two-hour AC interruption. Limits: Laboratory exposure, not measured real-centre attendance or mortality prevention; transient response, not all-day protection. Meade et al.: laboratory cooling-centre simulation (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    AC, ventilation and operations require energy; incremental peak demand depends on whether existing conditioned space or new equipment is used. No kWh estimate inferred.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    Actual facility refrigerants/charges and GWP not disclosed; assess equipment, leakage and grid emissions separately.

    In a power cut

    Existing facilities still depend on functioning power; a published refuge designation does not establish backup capacity.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Cooling can add electricity demand, charging/refrigeration needs and waste heat outside the protected zone. What helps: Reduce exposure and envelope heat gain, use appropriate efficient cooling, maintain access and test actual energy demand; do not substitute gadgets for work-rest protection.

    For the poorest

    Purchase and recurrent costs as a share of income were not published in reviewed sources. Do not infer affordability or free access. Assess transport, missed earnings and maintenance/charging costs.

    Known opening times, free/affordable practical access, transport/outreach, accessibility, staffing, electricity and escalation arrangements are funded.

    What could stop it

    Distance, hot journeys, stigma, entry requirements, night closure, care obligations, pets, crowding or power failure.

    Rough cost

    No verified installed/local lifecycle price in the opened sources; affordability adjectives in abstracts are not accepted as price evidence.

    City and local governments, Health authorities, Community and civil society groups, Utilities and energy regulators, Development banks, donors and climate funds. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed responsibility: employer for required occupational protection; facility/public authority for shared public cooling. Confirm recurrent budget and access arrangements; no funding commitment implied.

    Fairness and risks

    Assess language, documentation, women’s safety, disability access, toilets, seating, accompaniment and income lost while attending. Public listing does not establish actual uptake; cooling-centre access cannot replace safe homes or overnight protection.

    Where it has been tried

    • Reported, not evaluated Bangkok, Thailand, 2026 policy record checked October 2026. AC rooms in schools, health centres, recreation facilities and district offices. Multiple municipal facilities; no single reconciled current count retained Bangkok Metropolitan Administration cooling-centre policy record (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Seoul, Republic of Korea, 2024 city announcement. Shared cooled refuges intended to address limited daytime access. Convenience-store trial network; no health outcome count Seoul Metropolitan Government: climate shelters (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Simulation or test Laboratory experiment simulated a cooling-centre visit; physiological changes are not programme evaluation. Meade et al.: laboratory cooling-centre simulation (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Official Bangkok record describes air-conditioned public rooms in existing municipal facilities and expansion plans; implementation/targets are kept separate. Bangkok Metropolitan Administration cooling-centre policy record (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated City describes convenience-store climate shelters, including the reason for extending access beyond daytime. Seoul Metropolitan Government: climate shelters (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer the service-design lesson, not Canadian laboratory effect size or Seoul costs; co-design routes and hours with local users.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Asian municipal programmes exist; a lab study shows transient physiological relief.

    Inferred: Shared cooling may extend access where household AC is unaffordable, if the complete service is reachable and usable.

    Uncertain: Real-world morbidity/mortality effect, inclusive uptake, current site-by-site hours and recurrent cost were not verified here.

    How it works

    Dry or humid heat

    Energy

    This mechanism can influence cooling demand or equipment choice; no watts or kWh apply to a policy itself and no achieved savings are assumed.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No single refrigerant or GWP belongs to this mechanism. Equipment procurement/standards need explicit efficiency, refrigerant safety, leakage and end-of-life requirements; no zero-emissions claim.

    In a power cut

    The mechanism is not an outage backup. Any cooling equipment financed or regulated still depends on its specified electricity supply unless a separately verified backup exists.

    The cooling-trap risk

    More efficient or easier-to-finance cooling can still increase total electricity use and outdoor heat rejection if appliance ownership, size or operating hours grow. What helps: Combine efficiency and refrigerant provisions with passive demand reduction, appropriate sizing, operational practices and equitable access.

    For the poorest

    Check actual access, recurring bills and exclusion of tenants, informal workers or households without a qualifying connection. Efficiency or credit availability alone does not establish affordability.

    Assign deliverables, budgets, accountable agencies and monitoring; align refrigerant and energy-efficiency policies.

    A publication without funded implementation or progress data is insufficient evidence of delivery.

    • Independently evaluated Senegal ECOFRIDGES, LaunchedApril2021; evaluatedMay2024. Evaluation confirms a bill-linked mechanism and identifies operational incentives and recycling constraints; appliance sales are not automatically financed installations. Country pilot for refrigerators/ACs UNEP Evaluation Office, independent terminal evaluation of Cooling Project (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Ouachita Electric, Arkansas, USA, Testimonyprepared2019-01-28. Utility CEO describes tariff-based upgrades including high-efficiency air-conditioning; primary implementer testimony is not an independent evaluation. HELP tariffed efficiency programme Ouachita Electric CEO testimony, Missouri Public Service Commission (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Independently evaluated Independent evaluation of the named programme, not an experimental proof that the mechanism always works. UNEP Evaluation Office, independent terminal evaluation of Cooling Project (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Supports the specific policy status or programme example stated; not a measured temperature or savings claim. UNEP U4E, ECOFRIDGES financial mechanisms (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Supports the specific policy status or programme example stated; not a measured temperature or savings claim. Ouachita Electric CEO testimony, Missouri Public Service Commission (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer institutional functions rather than legal thresholds, finance terms or savings percentages. Check current jurisdiction-specific law, enforcement capacity, tariffs, appliance availability, consumer protection and informal housing access.

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: An independent evaluation and primary utility testimony verify distinct bill/tariff-linked mechanisms.

    Inferred: Cost recovery can support access if payments are affordable and service/consumer protections function.

    Uncertain: Current loan terms, universal bill savings, default/disconnection effects and transfer to informal Asian households are not established.
