    Indoor temperature and humidity monitoring linked to an action protocolActive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyMeasure indoor conditions where people spend time and connect the readings to locally agreed actions such as reducing heat gain, changing the occupied space or escalating support.

    How it works

    Measure indoor conditions where people spend time and connect the readings to locally agreed actions such as reducing heat gain, changing the occupied space or escalating support. A temperature/RH sensor observes exposure; it does not diagnose heat illness or measure all thermal loads.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Monitoring and response controls apply in both climates, but measured conditions and local response rules differ. This measure itself does not cool air or people.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Monitoring is documented and recommended as a decision aid; no isolated cooling, illness or mortality reduction attributable to sensor installation was verified. England guidance; Bangladesh field measurement, 2022 field data;2025–2026 publications. See examples; guidance is not an intervention sample. Limits: Measuring conditions and evaluating protection are different tasks. Air temperature/RH do not capture all radiant, airflow, metabolic or clothing factors. UKHSA heat-health alert action card: health/social care providers (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Device and communications energy depends on instrument, logging and network choice; no wattage verified. Monitoring is not a substitute for cooling-system power or an action budget.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No refrigerant is intrinsic to a thermometer/logger or monitoring protocol. Embodied electronics, batteries and any triggered cooling actions still have impacts.

    In a power cut

    Specify whether readings, logging and alerts work during outages; battery/local readout may avoid dependence on connectivity, but cooling or referral still needs a functioning service. No backup duration verified.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Information alone can legitimise ineffective action, or trigger inefficient cooling without addressing exposure and access. What helps: Link readings to practical protection, passive load reduction and appropriately efficient cooling; evaluate delivery rather than dashboard activity.

    For the poorest

    Proposed shared/public provision rather than requiring vulnerable households or workers to buy and maintain instruments. Income shares and affordability were not verified.

    What makes it work

    Instrument placement represents actual occupancy, readings are understood, and someone has the authority/resources to act. UKHSA recommends arrangements for staff and those receiving care.

    What could stop it

    Equipment without a response owner, inaccessible or unrepresentative locations, unmaintained sensors and no available cooler space can break the action pathway.

    Rough cost

    Comparable device, calibration, replacement and staff-response costs not disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed implementation arrangement: named facility/safety staff maintain instruments and logs, check batteries and calibration against the relevant instrument/standard, and review the response protocol. No universal frequency or device service life verified.

    Who acts

    Health authorities, Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: responsible employer or facility/public-service budget with support for resource-constrained settings. No funding commitment inferred.

    Fairness and risks

    Check who is measured, who sees the readings, accessible language/displays, consent for identifiable household data and who can access protection. Do not make assistance conditional on a sensor score or transfer unpaid monitoring duties to women without agreement.

    Where it has been tried

    • Measured in a study Chakaria, coastal Bangladesh, 16 March–8 May2022; published6June2025. Observational research established an indoor exposure-measurement workflow. It did not test a cooling response triggered by the sensors. 49 indoor temperature/RH loggers;490 household survey, with one logger extrapolated to neighbouring households of similar materials McGirr et al. Indoor heat and acute symptom reporting, Chakaria (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Southwark, London, England, Local2023 preparedness work reported in May2025 JSNA; exact card distribution date not stated. Homecare staff received thermometer cards for vulnerable clients and hot-weather information. Detailed evaluation was not completed. Number of cards/recipients not reported in reviewed section Southwark Council Hot Weather and Health JSNA (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Official guidance or data Official action card connects room-temperature monitoring and staff readiness to heat-response planning; applies to England, not a universal temperature rule. UKHSA heat-health alert action card: health/social care providers (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Chakaria research used indoor temperature/RH loggers to characterise exposure; it was observational, not a trial of a monitoring-triggered protection protocol. McGirr et al. Indoor heat and acute symptom reporting, Chakaria (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Reported, not evaluated Council reports thermometer cards distributed through homecare staff, alongside information; detailed project evaluation had not been completed. Southwark Council Hot Weather and Health JSNA (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Use local indoor measurements and service capacity; retain humidity and broader heat-load context where relevant. Clinical judgement and local protocols take priority over importing an English room-temperature trigger.

    Other sources

    • HSE Thermal comfort: environmental and personal factors (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: Monitoring components have been used in Bangladesh research and Southwark homecare activity. Official guidance links measurement to action; neither example establishes the independent effect of the complete proposed package.

    Inferred: Taxonomy, suggested actors/payers and transfer screens are analytical mappings.

    Uncertain: Isolated mortality/illness benefits, lifecycle prices and implementation fidelity not established.

    Related practical actions: Homes · Outdoor and hot workplaces · Schools and childcare · Health facilities

    Worksite WBGT monitoring linked to heat protectionActive coolingDry and humid heatMeasured in a studyMeasure worksite heat load with a wet-bulb globe temperature assessment and use it with workload, clothing/PPE, acclimatisation and worker condition to select protective actions.

    How it works

    Measure worksite heat load with a wet-bulb globe temperature assessment and use it with workload, clothing/PPE, acclimatisation and worker condition to select protective actions. WBGT is an environmental index, not body temperature, ordinary weather wet-bulb temperature or a guarantee of safety.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Monitoring and response controls apply in both climates, but measured conditions and local response rules differ. This measure itself does not cool air or people.

    What it has done

    • qualitative guidance Worksite monitoring is an input to exposure reduction and response. No standalone reduction in temperature, injury or mortality attributable solely to a WBGT meter was verified. Singapore framework; Qatar study; US guidance, 2019–2026. Qatar125 workers across two sites; Singapore framework not a study sample. Limits: Worksite conditions, clothing, workload and acclimatisation alter interpretation; do not export a single legal or safety threshold. NIOSH Heat Safety Tool App and WBGT limitations (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Energy

    Device and communications energy depends on instrument, logging and network choice; no wattage verified. Monitoring is not a substitute for cooling-system power or an action budget.

    Refrigerant and emissions

    No refrigerant is intrinsic to a thermometer/logger or monitoring protocol. Embodied electronics, batteries and any triggered cooling actions still have impacts.

    In a power cut

    Specify whether readings, logging and alerts work during outages; battery/local readout may avoid dependence on connectivity, but cooling or referral still needs a functioning service. No backup duration verified.

    The cooling-trap risk

    Information alone can legitimise ineffective action, or trigger inefficient cooling without addressing exposure and access. What helps: Link readings to practical protection, passive load reduction and appropriately efficient cooling; evaluate delivery rather than dashboard activity.

    For the poorest

    Proposed shared/public provision rather than requiring vulnerable households or workers to buy and maintain instruments. Income shares and affordability were not verified.

    What makes it work

    Measurements represent actual tasks/locations, staff interpret them competently, and work-rest, hydration, shade, acclimatisation and emergency arrangements can be enacted.

    What could stop it

    A weather-app reading may miss a local radiant source or microclimate; no stop/escalation authority, paid-rest arrangement or functioning protection can leave monitoring without benefit.

    Rough cost

    Comparable device, calibration, replacement and staff-response costs not disclosed in reviewed sources; no universal price inferred.

    Upkeep

    Proposed implementation arrangement: named facility/safety staff maintain instruments and logs, check batteries and calibration against the relevant instrument/standard, and review the response protocol. No universal frequency or device service life verified.

    Who acts

    Health authorities, Employers and businesses, Worker organisations and unions, Schools and education authorities, Community and civil society groups. Suggested, not commitments.

    Who pays

    Proposed: responsible employer or facility/public-service budget with support for resource-constrained settings. No funding commitment inferred.

    Fairness and risks

    Include subcontracted, migrant and informal workers; ensure accessible warnings and a non-punitive route to rest or stop. Do not use a reading to override symptoms or force work. Worker control, pay consequences and data handling require local agreement.

    Where it has been tried

    • Official guidance or data Singapore outdoor workplaces, Frameworkcurrent27October2026; four additional mandatory practices announced for1December2026. Official framework connects WBGT monitoring with graduated protection and emergency planning. This is a verified policy mechanism, not evidence that every worksite has complied or an independent outcome evaluation. On-site meters required for specified construction, shipyard and process-sector workplaces; framework does not report installation count Singapore Ministry of Manpower: heat stress measures for outdoor work (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study A construction site and a farm, Qatar, Summer2019. Environmental, physiological, work and perception data accompanied tests of hydration, clothing and work-rest measures. Findings cannot isolate the monitoring device as the causal intervention. 125 study participants;5,500work hours across two worksites; site workforce is not the study sample FAME Laboratory for ILO: occupational heat strain and mitigation in Qatar (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    • Official guidance or data NIOSH recommends WBGT for occupational assessment and states that WBGT or heat index alone cannot prevent heat stress; heat index is not interchangeable with full worksite assessment. NIOSH Heat Safety Tool App and WBGT limitations (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Singapore ministry specifies WBGT monitoring and protection measures; the page distinguishes existing requirements from changes effective1December2026. Singapore Ministry of Manpower: heat stress measures for outdoor work (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Measured in a study Independent University of Thessaly field research examined environmental and physiological conditions alongside mitigation; monitoring was one component, not a standalone intervention. FAME Laboratory for ILO: occupational heat strain and mitigation in Qatar (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Moving it elsewhere

    Adapt instrument selection, measurement positions, worker consultation and action protocols to local solar/process heat, clothing, workload and acclimatisation. Weather wet-bulb temperature is not WBGT; do not present an app or a single threshold as worker clearance.

    Other sources

    • NIOSH Workplace recommendations (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • WHO-WMO occupational heat stress guidance launch (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Known, inferred, uncertain

    Known: An official Singapore monitoring/action framework exists, and Qatar field research tested a wider protection package with heat assessment. Monitoring is not itself cooling.

    Inferred: Taxonomy, suggested actors/payers and transfer screens are analytical mappings.

    Uncertain: Isolated mortality/illness benefits, lifecycle prices and implementation fidelity not established.

    Comparable local implementation cost not verified. Benefit transfers, insurance premiums, programme envelopes and appropriations are different financial flows; see financial_flows when available.

    Upkeep

    Institutional arrangements require continued staffing, records, operating funds and review; no universal service life or quantified upkeep interval verified.

    Who acts

    Utilities and energy regulators, Water authorities, National governments, City and local governments. Suggested, not commitments.

    Where it has been tried

    • Official guidance or data Arizona, United States, 2026-06-02. Regulator describes summer and heat-triggered disconnection restrictions. Arizona regulator summer disconnection protection (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Official guidance or data Washington, United States, Current text includes2026amendment. Law protects covered district-utility customers during heat-related alerts. Washington RCW54.16.285 heat-alert utility protections (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Evidence

    Moving it elsewhere

    Transfer the function and operating questions, not another jurisdiction’s legal duties, benefit amount, thresholds, costs or effectiveness. Verify local climate, service capacity, rights, access and recurrent funding.

    Procure and verify an operating protection servicePlans, work and moneyDry and humid heatOfficial guidance or dataContract for service hours, staffing, maintenance and performance reporting, not just asset delivery.

    How it works

    Contract for service hours, staffing, maintenance and performance reporting, not just asset delivery.

    Dry or humid heat

    Dry and humid heat. Institutional/service measure; adapt local risk thresholds to humidity, hot nights, duration, exposure and population. This is not a physical cooling-performance claim.

    What it has done

    • qualitative; see evidence kind and example status Documented mechanism, guidance or delivery example; attributable exposure/health/income effect not verified for this standalone measure. See examples, See examples. Not verified for a standalone effect. Limits: A plan, payment, service output or duty is not evidence of causal protection.

    Who owns it

    • Phoenix, United States: City departments and contracted providers
    • India highway construction/maintenance: NHAI and contractors

    Legal basis

    • Phoenix, United States: Not verified; publication/activity does not establish a statutory duty.
    • India highway construction/maintenance: Not verified; publication/activity does not establish a statutory duty.

    Where the money comes from

    • Phoenix, United States: Not publicly disclosed in reviewed source.
    • India highway construction/maintenance: Not publicly disclosed in reviewed source.

    What sets it off

    Procurement/renewal, service failure and inspection results.

    Who it reaches

    Users included in contracted protection and opening hours.

    Who may be missed: Unserved settlements; informal workers outside contracts.

    What makes it work

    Clear service levels, paid upkeep and a public route to report failures.

    What could stop it

    Procurement accepts installed assets without testing delivery.

    Combinations that work together

    No single measure protects people on its own. These are proposed combinations, by setting, in the order they are usually put in place. They are designs to test, not proven packages.

    Design conceptHomes

    Cooler homes with protection through the night

    1. Agree tenant/owner permissions and identify residents unable to leave.
    2. Measure occupied-room day/night heat and inspect roof structure, leaks and wiring.
    3. Select shading/roof treatment and ventilation appropriate to outside conditions.
    4. Provide conditional fan use, targeted cooled refuge and an outage fallback.
    5. Assign cleaning, repairs, electricity support and review after the hot season.

    Made of: Solar-reflective roof coatings · External fabric awnings · Cross ventilation through connected openings · Efficient BLDC ceiling fans · Night-time and round-the-clock outreach with heat escalation

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Design conceptOutdoor and hot workplaces

    Protected work with income continuity

    1. Map tasks, metabolic workload, clothing and vulnerable workers with worker representatives.
    2. Provide accessible shade, drinking water, toilets and recovery space before warnings.
    3. Agree locally competent exposure limits, paid recovery, workload changes and stop-work authority.
    4. Train supervisors and workers, establish referral and grievance routes.
    5. Audit actual rest taken, income retained and health outcomes.

    Made of: Public shade structures, sails and market/queue canopies · Worksite WBGT monitoring linked to heat protection · Mechanically cooled worker rest shelter · Paid rest, shade and drinking-water protocols · Worker stop-work rights and heat grievance channels

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Design conceptOutdoor and hot workplacesMarkets and neighbourhoods

    Markets and informal livelihoods with physical and financial protection

    1. Co-design with vendor/home-worker organisations and identify permission constraints.
    2. Install maintainable shade and accessible water/rest amenities without obstructing movement.
    3. Define an affordable income-protection route and data/trigger responsibilities.
    4. Test payout channels and a non-insurance fallback for harmful non-trigger heat.
    5. Review who received help, timing, adequacy and debt stress.

    Made of: Public shade structures, sails and market/queue canopies · Parametric heat insurance for income shocks · A fallback funding layer when an index misses real harm · Heat-triggered cash outside an insurance contract

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Design conceptSchools and childcare

    Learning continuity with safer classrooms

    1. Map classroom exposure, water, disability access and childcare dependencies.
    2. Repair shade and roof defects and test climate-appropriate ventilation.
    3. Add efficient air movement or targeted cooling where assessment supports it.
    4. Agree authority for escalating protection, changed timetables and continuity support.
    5. Check attendance, indoor heat, care burdens and upkeep.

    Made of: Schoolyard greening, depaving and shade as a coordinated retrofit · External fabric awnings · Solar-reflective roof coatings · Efficient BLDC ceiling fans · Closure decisions with offline learning continuity · School heat operating plans, water access and escalation

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Design conceptHealth facilities

    Heat-ready clinics with dependable services

    1. Audit patient/staff exposure, water, cold-chain and critical circuits.
    2. Reduce heat gain; define clinical cooling needs with qualified facility staff.
    3. Size efficient cooling and backup to verified loads; test outages and referral.
    4. Fund staff surge, access to care, service contracts and heat surveillance.
    5. Review failures, clinical outcomes and operating costs after each season.

    Made of: External fabric awnings · Resilient power for health-facility cooling and cold-chain loads · Solar-direct-drive vaccine refrigeration · Heat-ready clinic protocols and staff capability · Heat surge staffing, triage and referral coordination · All-cause and excess-mortality analysis for heat attribution

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Design conceptMarkets and neighbourhoods

    Neighbourhood refuge, access and trusted outreach

    1. Map journeys, hot-night vulnerability and access with residents.
    2. Provide immediate shade and a reachable refuge while longer-term trees establish.
    3. Test opening hours, water, transport, toilets, accessibility and outage fallback.
    4. Use consent-based outreach with trusted local-language intermediaries.
    5. Monitor use, missed access, tree survival and displacement indicators.

    Made of: Street trees and retained mature canopy · Public shade structures, sails and market/queue canopies · Public air-conditioned cooling centre or shared refuge · Disability-inclusive outreach, communication and referral · Consent-based registers and check-ins for isolated people · Night-time and round-the-clock outreach with heat escalation

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Design conceptOutdoor and hot workplacesMarkets and neighbourhoods

    Farm and agricultural-worker protection

    1. Assess worker/livestock exposure, crop response and seasonal water constraints.
    2. Provide mobile shade, safe water and rest/workload arrangements immediately.
    3. Test crop-compatible shade/agroforestry and livestock shelter with local expertise.
    4. Link advisories to agreed actions and realistic income/credit safeguards.
    5. Monitor worker health, yields, water withdrawals and maintenance.

    Made of: Shade-tree agroforestry for crops · Artificial shade shelters for livestock · Mobile shaded rest shelters for agricultural workers · Paid rest, shade and drinking-water protocols · Reschedule work and reduce peak-heat task exposure

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Design conceptBefore summer: for municipalities

    Before-summer delivery platform

    1. Appoint accountable sector owners and include worker/community representatives.
    2. Translate vulnerability evidence into a costed place portfolio and service standards.
    3. Agree forecast triggers, spending authority, procurement and backup arrangements.
    4. Rehearse offline warnings, cash delivery, clinics, water and electricity contingencies.
    5. Publish implementation data and review outcomes and exclusion after the season.

    Made of: Heat action plans with a seasonal responsibility matrix · Pre-agreed heat anticipatory action and forecast finance · Dedicated and traceable heat operating budgets · Heatwave grid-readiness planning and emergency resource coordination

    Researcher-proposed combination; component evidence does not establish complete-package effectiveness.

    Blind spots

    Harms that are rarely counted, and what to measure so they are not missed.

    • Indoor heat. Home exposure, roof access, kitchen heat and actual occupied-room conditions; outdoor weather cannot substitute for indoor measurements. Reported, not evaluated Build Change/KOMIDA incremental heat adaptation (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Night heat and isolated older people. Track night recovery, access to help and power reliability; do not assume daytime refuges meet nighttime needs. Official guidance or data WHO Heat and health (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Women’s unpaid care and home-based work. Include unpaid hours, care travel and the ability to use cooling; this source is a programme account, not a population estimate. Reported, not evaluated Build Change/KOMIDA incremental heat adaptation (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Informal workers and migrants. Measure income loss, identity/language barriers and inability to stop work; migrant-specific coverage in this synthesis is limited. Reported, not evaluated CGAP account of SEWA heat protection (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Mental health. WHO recognises heat-related mental-health risks; evaluated local protective packages were not established here. Official guidance or data WHO Heat and health (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Kidney injury from strenuous work. Track repeated occupational exposure and relevant clinical outcomes; benefits in one sugarcane cohort do not establish every occupation’s response. Measured in a study Nicaragua rest–shade–hydration–hygiene cohort (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Disability and access. Eligibility does not prove accessible delivery; measure transport, information formats, caregiver needs and actual receipt. Reported, not evaluated Bangladesh early-action protocol case (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Deaths beyond certified heatstroke. Mortality time-series analysis can illuminate broader heat-associated harm; attributable estimates and recorded heatstroke deaths answer different questions. Measured in a study Ahmedabad heat-action-plan mortality analysis (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Operational and institutional budget lines. Maintenance, data, coordination, paid recovery and local intermediaries are priorities for further funding research; no global funding-allocation claim is established. Measured in a study CPR assessment of Indian heat action plans (opens in a new tab) ↗

    Worth watching

    New ideas, labelled honestly by how far they have got.

    • Simulation or test Radiative-cooling paint with transparent negative findings (2024). Outdoor aluminium-box experiments; no observed subambient cooling. Watch for: Occupied-building heat and health, humidity/cloud effects, weathering, material safety and installed cost. Radiative-cooling paint experimental preprint (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Anticipatory social-protection delivery rehearsal (2025). Actual institutional simulation rather than a proven heat-emergency impact. Watch for: Real-event payment timing, false alarms, excluded residents and income adequacy. Rajshahi anticipatory social-protection simulation (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Simulation or test Technical assistance linked to incremental home adaptation (Pilot launched 2025; account 2026). Programme pilot reported by implementer; not independent outcome evaluation. Watch for: Indebtedness, tenant reach, thermal performance, repayment during lost income and maintenance. Build Change/KOMIDA incremental heat adaptation (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Design concept Cooling finance for informal food vendors (2026 announcement). Funded project design; deployment and results not verified in announcement. Watch for: Worker agency, demand, food safety, maintenance, trigger failure and repayment affordability. ClimateWorks extreme-heat grantee announcement (opens in a new tab) ↗
    • Design concept Participatory structural heat adaptation trial (Listed ongoing at October 2026 check; start date not verified). Trial design officially listed; recruitment or installed intervention status not established here. Watch for: Confirm registration, dates, protocol, measured outcomes and adverse-event reporting before changing label. SHAPES structural adaptation trial (opens in a new tab) ↗
